title: Swans prevail in AFLW elimination final scrap against Bulldogs
text:
AFLW superstar Chloe Molloy has once again lifted Sydney to victory, with the Swans defeating the Western Bulldogs by 29 points in an elimination final.

League-leading goalkicker Molloy pulled off a surprise cameo down back to help the Swans claim a 7.4 (46) to 2.5 (17) win at a wet and windy Henson Park on Sunday.

Sydney will next play Geelong in an away semi-final. The Bulldogs' season is over.

Molloy's leadership in a wet-weather scrap proved the difference for the Swans, with the former Swans co-skipper finishing with one goal, 12 intercepts, and 14 contested possessions.

Tanya Kennedy was just as crucial for the Swans, locking down Bulldogs co-captain and gun midfielder Isabelle Pritchard.

Pritchard, on return from a knee injury, was kept to just 14 disposals and three clearances as Kennedy laid 17 tackles.

Fellow Bulldogs midfielder Ellie Blackburn, also returning after being rested in last week's loss to the Cats, led the visitors with 29 touches and a goal.

Swans captain Lucy McEvoy needed just 20 seconds to score the opener with a long bomb from outside the 50-metre arc thanks to the strong breeze.

A rushed behind gave the Bulldogs their sole score of the first quarter, as the hosts made the most of conditions to fire off their four unanswered goals and build a 24-point lead.

The Bulldogs could only manage one point with the breeze in the second, with Molloy helping limit the damage with five contested possessions and four intercepts as a defender.

Molloy's stint in defence forced Bulldogs coach Tam Hyett to bring defender Vaomua Laloifi into the forward line, and the pair's battle continued well into the second half.

Sunday's final turned into a slog after torrential rain came in the third quarter, with the Swans doing just enough to maintain a 25-point lead en route to victory in front of 4,325 dedicated fans.

AAP

title: Residents bought into communities but may end up living in 'wastelands'
text:
Rinnah Roque worries the view beyond her landscaped front garden will remain a construction site.

The 60-year-old committed to a growing community in Sydney's north-west when she bought a three-storey townhouse off the plan in Box Hill.

Across the road, a hive of builders were working on 47 homes as part of a project from the developer Bathla.

"I worked so hard to be able to buy a property for my mum and myself," she said.

" I was hoping that houses would be built as quickly as possible. You want to live in a community. "

Construction work on Hynds Road stopped after Bathla entered administration. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

But for the past two months, the symphony of construction noise has been replaced by silence.

"All of a sudden everything stopped, and what's so frustrating is everything was just left behind," she said.

The residential development dividing Hynds Road is one of hundreds caught up in the $3.4 billion collapse of Bathla Group.

And it is among dozens of sites that were part way through construction when the money stopped flowing.

In some cases, the private equity companies that are owed money by Bathla have taken control of the projects they invested in, and are racing to find builders that will finish them.

The Box Hill development is among hundreds caught up in the collapse of Bathla Group. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

But interviews with experts and industry stakeholders reveal that builders may be reluctant to guarantee the work of cash-strapped Bathla, posing the risk some sites could "languish".

Bathla declined the ABC's requests for interview and comment.

Hurdles to finishing Bathla's projects

The quality of the work already undertaken at Bathla's construction sites would be difficult to assess by the builders that are considering finishing the projects, said Lyndall Bryant, a leading property economics professor at Queensland University of Technology.

"If you're a builder coming into a job that's half-finished, you don't want to be warranting the work that someone else has done," she said.

"If the concrete's been poured, you don't want to be saying, 'Oh yeah, I guarantee that that concrete's been done properly.'"

Lyndall Bryant says some builders may be hesitant to take on half-finished jobs. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

She said reviewing plumbing or electrical work would be challenging if walls were already erected.

A private equity company that spoke to the ABC but declined to be named said the builders it was talking to were being cautious however, it remained confident one would be appointed.

Bathla's land deals ahead of collapse A former major lender says Bathla was expanding too quickly, leaving it vulnerable when the property market turned.

Urban Taskforce Australia, a group lobbying for developers and equity financiers, said it believed most of the projects would be completed.

"Where I would be concerned is if we were to find developments with substantial defects, where basically the cost to rectify those defects is greater than the value of the land with an approval on it," chief executive Tom Forrest said.

"I can't see that being the case in lots of occasions."

Impact on home values

Bathla was forced to stop construction at 45 sites after it was placed into administration in August, according to documents filed by the administrator Teneo to the NSW Supreme Court.

About a dozen of these sites are situated in Sydney's west, in areas such as Marsden Park, Box Hill, Rouse Hill and Pemulwuy.

Many are in new areas, clustered together.

Developments at Marsden Park in Sydney's west are among those where construction has stopped. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

Professor Bryant said the delay or failure of a project in these locations could leave communities "fractured".

"Those areas really could become almost wastelands for a number of years," she said.

"These sites attract vandalism, they're not maintained, and it just brings down the whole area.

"Unfortunately it's a negative impact on property values — and that's for the people who already live in those communities."

Ms Roque said if this scenario were to eventuate in Box Hill, it would be "a horror story".

"That will impact probably us mentally and even the whole family," she said.

Rinnah Roque (left) says it would be a "horror story" if the area become a "wasteland". (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

Urban Taskforce Australia said any drop in property values would be a "short-term blip".

"My hope is that the fracturing of the community doesn't happen because ultimately the market will come in and complete those homes," Mr Forrest said.

Councils could be left footing the bill

Two Sydney councils are among the most exposed.

Construction had stopped on eight Bathla projects in Blacktown Council, and at four sites in The Hills Shire Council.

Both councils are owed money by Bathla, and have registered as creditors with the administrator.

The councils could be left spending more money while bringing in less.

The Hills Shire Council and Blacktown Council are the most exposed from the Bathla collapse. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

They might have to spend money building infrastructure such as roads and sewage that Bathla has yet to contribute to the developments, Professor Bryant said.

"Blacktown Council is at risk of having to spend significant money on infrastructure for projects that are on the fringe that might only service a few people," she said.

And they would be missing out on money they anticipated from rates, unless these developments are finished.

"I think that they should be concerned at Blacktown City Council because any major hiccup like this means delay in their cash flows," Mr Forrest said.

Blacktown Council declined a request for interview and comment.

The Hills Shire Council Mayor, Michelle Byrnes, said the collapse of Bathla was "another hit to public confidence in the construction industry".

Michelle Byrne says the public's confidence in the construction industry has been dealt another blow. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

"I'm devastated for the buyers across Sydney who have been left stranded by Bathla's collapse," she said.

Private equity investors race to recoup investments

Some investors have seized control of the Bathla sites they invested in and are racing to finish the projects.

One of them said the goal was to break even, with any profit considered a bonus.

Asian private equity company PAG has already appointed the builder ParkView to its 300-unit development in Pemulwuy.

Other private equity companies told the ABC they were in discussions with builders.

Major lender in Bathla development sells debts Private credit firms are striking deals to recover their money following the $3.4 billion collapse of property giant Bathla Group.

Ray White Capital, which owns the site in Box Hill, said it expected the site to be finished before April 2027.

Leda Group has taken control of a 240-unit development in Marsden Park, and said it was in advanced discussions with a builder.

But not all of Bathla's sites have been taken over by a creditor.

Among them is a 49-home housing estate in Lochinvar in the NSW Hunter Region.

The restructuring and insolvency firm Mackay Goodwin has been appointed to "assess available options".

title: Cancelled AI data centre 'victory for people power' after backlash
text:
Plans for another controversial AI data centre in Sydney have been scrapped, with a community group hailing the decision as a "victory for people power".

The facility, which was set to become part of a proposed logistics hub on the Cooks River at Arncliffe in the city's south, faced backlash from the local community after it was revealed in July last year.

Developers Stockland and John Boyd Properties proposed to redevelop the rezoned 18.3-hectare Kogarah Golf Club site into an estimated $3.5 billion logistics precinct including an AI data centre.

Stockland and John Boyd Properties withdrew their plans for the AI data centre. (Supplied)

Stop the Cooks River AI Project (SCRAP), which consists of hundreds of members, had been protesting against the development since forming in August.

'We were worried'

Group organiser Paddy Gibson said surrounding residents were celebrating the "very good win for people power".

"People really love this river and we're just horrified to hear that it could be threatened in this way," he said.

Mr Gibson said it would have posed a risk to the fragile local ecology around the river, which is called Goolay'yari in local Indigenous languages, which was already recovering from "industrialisation over the years".

"There's endangered plants and other animal species in the green space," he said.

"There's plenty of people trying to work on remediating what is a very polluted river, and we were worried that this would set back those efforts."

Paddy Gibson says there are endangered plants and other animal species at the proposed data centre site. (Supplied)

He also mentioned concerns about power usage and possible water contamination.

A Stockland spokesperson said the partners were now focused on building a "world class logistics precinct which does not include a data centre as part of the amended Concept Masterplan".

"The site is on the doorstep of Sydney Airport and in close proximity to Port Botany and major transport infrastructure, making it uniquely suited for a logistics hub and has potential for mixed uses, like retail and hospitality," they said.

"The project will also deliver a one-kilometre public foreshore link along the Cooks River and the future delivery of the 14-hectare Pemulwuy Park, as well as local road upgrades and improved active transport connections."

The spokesperson said the group would continue to engage openly with stakeholders as planning for the logistics precinct progressed.

'A wildlife sanctuary'

Bayside Greens councillor Peter Strong who had led council's opposition to the project said the decision was "very heartening".

Mr Strong said forums and outdoor events about the project had attracted large numbers of residents.

His main concerns were about excess energy and water use, noise, and the way AI was being "used and weaponised against the best wishes of humanity".

"That space has become a bit of a wildlife sanctuary since nothing much has happened with the old Kogarah Golf Club since they sold it," Mr Strong said.

Locals were concerned with the impact on water use and energy. (Supplied)

He said the withdrawal sent a message to the state government that "the council should have more of a veto on these data centres".

In August, the Minns government released its data centre policy framework which they said balanced the interests of households and investment in NSW.

A recent report following a parliamentary inquiry into data centres noted that the guidelines should have been in place "before developing any planning fast-track processes for these projects".

The government has until February next year to respond to the report.

Canterbury Labor MP Sophie Cotsis said she looked forward to seeing the revised logistics hub masterplan including a public foreshore link, road upgrades and improved active transport connections.

"The Minns Labor Government has established the Cooks River Consolidation Project to resolve longstanding tenure issues along the river," she said.

"As the local MP I am focused on working together with my colleagues and government agencies to see investment in the naturalisation of the river banks."

AI data centre pushback

Protesters at Merrylands rallying against a proposed AI data centre. (ABC News: Alex Lewis)

It is the latest in a series of proposed data centres to be scrapped following community opposition.

An AirTrunk data centre proposed in Lane Cove was also dropped, and another in Guildford in September.

Residents at Merrylands in Western Sydney have also rallied against the $1.1 billion Project Pluto Data Centre proposed by the Goodman Group, to be located next to the Guildford West Sportsground.

Labelled a state-significant development, locals said it was approved in July behind their backs.

The project did not receive a single submission from the public, with some locals saying they never received a letter.

Goodman Group said it had sent correspondence to more than 1,200 homes and businesses, three times.

SCRAP said it would continue campaigning against the logistics hub on the riverfront and for a ban on all new AI data centres.

title: Final Garage Sale Trail after 16 years of re-homing second-hand goods
text:
From casual beginnings in Bondi in 2010 to a nationwide annual event, the Garage Sale Trail has found a new home for more than seven million pre-loved items and, in doing so, generated $52 million for sellers.

It is a long way from what co-founder Darryl Nichols said started as a "smell of an oily rag production".

He and friend Andrew Valder called for community members in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs to host a second-hand sale.

To their surprise, 130 people signed up, and it grew from there.

The success and the impact are beyond anything they could have imagined.

Darryl Nichols co-founded the Garage Sale Trail in 2010. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

"Garage sales are a quintessential part of Australian culture," Mr Nichols said.

"They go along with Vegemite, going to the beach, watching the cricket in summer and all that good stuff.

"When the internet sort of started to kick in, in the late 90s and early 2000s, and we saw … marketplaces like eBay enter the game, maybe the humble old garage sale did take a bit of a hit.

"But we've certainly found over the years that the Garage Sale Trail provides a wonderful opportunity for people who have been thinking about having a garage sale but never sort of got around to doing it ."

More than 7.2 million second-hand items have been sold through the Garage Sale Trail since 2010. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

This year, the final event occurs across two weekends, with Sunday, November 15, to be the final day.

Mr Nichols said it was the right time to walk away.

"It's been such an incredible journey we feel like we've really made a big contribution to reuse and circularity in Australia," he said.

"Perhaps there's someone out there … that might be interested in taking on the custodianship of Garage Sale Trail … but we feel like we've made a strong contribution and we're ready for the next chapter."

Reducing landfill

According to the NSW Environment Protection Authority, Greater Sydney is on track to run out of landfill space by 2030 unless more is done to reduce waste.

In a statement, the EPA described the Garage Sale Trail as "a fantastic initiative that helps to divert waste from landfill and reduce illegal dumping by encouraging reuse as part of a circular economy."

From her garage sale at Kanwal on the NSW Central Coast, Kalie Chaney agreed.

"I honestly don't think I could work at a tip because it would break my heart seeing all the things people throw away," she said.

The NSW Environment Protection Authority says the Garage Sale Trail helped divert waste from landfill and reduce illegal dumping. (ABC Central Coast: Shauna Foley)

Ms Chaney collects items from the 1960s and 70s.

"Things were made to last back then … whether it's furniture or Tupperware or dinner plates, they are still usable," she said

"It's good to save them, because a lot of these items [would otherwise] go to landfill."

Community connection

Recycling and reuse aside, there is something about a garage sale that gets people talking.

Bill Mallie popped into Ms Chaney's garage sale for the social aspect.

"It brings neighbours together … it's a community thing," Mr Mallie said.

Bill Mallie says garage sales bring the community together. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

"At my age I need to get rid of stuff, I don't need to bring stuff in."

"[But] it's neighbours … helping each other clearing out stuff, recycling things [so] they don't wind up in the dump … what a great idea."

Mr Nichols said the social side of the movement has been almost as profound as its environmental side.

"The average person that gets involved makes about 30 new neighbourly connections through the day," he said.

Around 12,000 hosts are taking part in the final Garage Sale Trail. (ABC Central Coast: Shauna Foley)

"When you have a garage sale … people drop their guard a little bit because you're putting all this stuff out the front of your house, it kind of says a little bit about who you are and provides this lovely opportunity for people to connect."

"At the end of the day, it's the contribution it's made to keeping perfectly great stuff out of landfill and bringing local people together that probably is the real win for our nation."

title: Chronic pain affects one in two women in midlife, report finds
text:
Women are up to 70 per cent more likely to experience chronic pain than men, according to a recent report from the international Menopause Society (IMS).

Chronic pain is pain that lasts more than three months, or keeps recurring.

In women, these pain symptoms often appear in midlife, likely due to factors such as fluctuating hormones, menopause-related biological shifts, lack of sleep and lifestyle changes.

Loading...

The IMS report estimates about half of all middle-aged women experience chronic pain, describing the condition as "often under-recognised, underdiagnosed and inadequately treated".

Rossella Nappi, IMS president and obstetrician and gynaecologist at the University of Pavia in Italy, says the report aims to empower women and health workers to talk about the condition.

"Chronic pain in midlife is a very important subject and highly neglected," she says.

"Sometimes the pain becomes widespread and it's present in every day of their life."

So what do we know about chronic pain in women and what can people do to minimise the severity of their symptoms?

Why is chronic pain more common in women?

We don't know for sure.

Adelaide University senior lecturer in pain science Jane Chalmers says this is one of the "hardest questions to answer" in her field.

"Trying to understand why certain people or certain groups are more vulnerable to others is often multi-factorial and very layered," she says.

"And that's because we can't separate a human's psychology and sociology from their biology."

Women often experience multiple, overlapping chronic pain syndromes, such as fibromyalgia and chronic pelvic pain.

While not everyone feels pain in the same way, some research suggests women may be more likely than men to experience central sensitisation, making the brain more likely to produce pain signals.

Nicolette Ellis wants women's chronic pain to be taken seriously, with many patients currently feeling dismissed. (Supplied)

And then there are social factors.

Chronic Pain Australia chair Nicollette Ellis, who is also a pharmacist specialising in chronic pain, says women often manage the majority of caregiving responsibilities, which may add to stress levels.

The relationship between stress and chronic pain is complex, but stress may worsen pain intensity for some people.

Why do these changes happen in midlife?

Hormones play a role.

During menopause, which marks the end of a woman's reproductive years, the body produces much lower amounts of oestrogen and progesterone.

Lower levels of oestrogen can lead to joint pain, stiffness and weakening of muscles.

Nearly three in four women experience joint or muscle pain during perimenopause. (Pexels: Kampus Production)

But these hormone levels can fluctuate day-to-day, explains Royal Australian College of General Practitioners menopause health subgroup chair Sharon Vasey.

This fluctuation can lead to migraines, she says.

But it's not all about hormones. Professor Nappi says lifestyle factors also play a key role in how we age.

"If we do not exercise properly, if we don't eat adequately and if we are not active very much in our life, pain will be an issue," she says.

"If we have menopausal symptoms, such as sleep disturbances, for example, or mood changes, this will affect the experience of the pain."

What type of pain do women report?

The IMS report focuses on three common symptoms: musculoskeletal pain, migraine and pelvic pain.

According to the report, nearly three in four women experience joint or muscle pain during perimenopause.

But figures from Chronic Pain Australia's 2026 National Pain Report paint a more complex picture.

The group surveyed more than 6,000 Australians, finding women experience an average of 4.6 different types of chronic pain, such as migraines, back, pelvic, joint or nerve pain.

With so many women reporting multiple symptoms, Ms Ellis says it's important not to treat types of pain in a "silo", but to consider the whole body and how different systems interact.

What can women do about it?

For women approaching midlife, Dr Vasey says it's important to get enough sleep, stay active and eat a healthy diet.

She says the first step for people experiencing pain symptoms is to speak to their GP.

"There's lots of things that can be done, women don't have to put up with chronic pain," she says.

New menopause treatment guidelines Australia has a new set of guidelines for managing the symptoms of menopause, that include hot flushes, night sweats, and a frequent need to urinate. Here's what it means for you.

Dr Vasey, who is also a practising GP, says menopausal hormone therapy can help ease the severity of some symptoms for some women, but medication isn't the only option.

It can also be helpful to see an allied health worker, such as a physiotherapist.

As many people with chronic pain experienced a delayed diagnosis, Ms Ellis says it is important health workers take pain symptoms seriously.

"The earlier we can treat [chronic pain] the better the outcomes," she says.

And a broader level, Monash University professor of occupational rheumatology Karen Walker-Bone says more needs to be done to support women approaching midlife.

This means making sure women have the financial stability to retire when they want, and to ensure emotional household labour is shared in an equitable way.

title: Rising female footy star dreams of playing NRLW
text:
Growing up with a house full of brothers, Elexis Riley was never going to be far from a game of footy.

While some teenagers are still figuring out what they want to be, the 16-year-old from coal country in central Queensland is already dreaming of one day competing in the National Rugby League Women's (NRLW) premiership.

"I just love the aggression in the game and how all the girls come together as a team and we play for each other," she said.

Five years ago, Riley's family moved from Rockhampton to Moranbah.

Despite living in the small regional coal-mining town with a population of just under 9,000, she's still had a lot of opportunities, from playing in the local league to being selected to play in representative competitions.

Elexis Riley (right) with the winning trophy from the 2026 season, playing for her local team, the under-17s Moranbah Miners rugby league team. (Supplied: Elexis Riley)

Elexis plays for the Moranbah Miners in the under-16 girls competition and just finished the 2026 season as the leading try scorer, crossing the line 17 times.

That followed a breakout season in 2025, which saw her picked for the Mackay Cutters under-15 girls academy.

Her footy has even taken her overseas. She's just returned home from a tour program with independent sports organisation Wanderers Australia, where she represented her country against teams in the United Kingdom.

"It was really good, we thought the teams were going to be a lot harder, but they were really easy to play," Elexis said.

Elexis Riley playing against Culcheth Eagles in England. (Supplied: Wanderers Australia)

But the biggest win of her sporting career so far has been her selection for the under-17s North Queensland Cowboys Academy in Townsville.

"It's actually wonderful … I was not expecting to take my footy this far … everything opened up to me and I had so many opportunities," she said.

Cowboys headquarters is 550 kilometres from home but she's been able to take part in the program remotely.

"They give us training and we have to do all of our gym work and stuff to keep up," Elexis said.

"And they can track us on how we go and then we go back there at the end of December."

While it's a bit to juggle on top of her year 11 schoolwork, she manages to get most of it done.

"I just try to do it at school and try my best [to do it all]," she said.

The remote training is a way the Cowboys team can spread the program to Queensland's many vast regions.

Ty Williams moved into the role of NRLW senior assistant and development coach of women's elite pathways at the North Queensland Cowboys two years ago.

"We thought, as staff here, instead of bringing all the athletes to us, which we do once or twice a year …. to get out there and see them in their own environment as well," Mr Williams said.

"Our main focus is how do we provide an opportunity for those young female athletes within our region to progress through to the highest level."

He said partnerships with local feeder clubs the Northern Pride, Townsville Blackhawks, Mackay Cutters and the Central Queensland Capras were integral.

"It's important to know that the progression or the pipeline for them to achieve the NRLW dream is through [those] clubs," Mr Williams said.

With attention already turning towards the 2027 competition, the young players will head into pre-season training over the next couple of weeks.

"The ultimate goal is to have our pathways programs playing against the likes of the Broncos and the Titans moving forward and potentially Redcliffe," Mr Williams said.

" We've got the big dreams ahead, but we know that we've got to progress slowly and make sure we provide an opportunity for these ladies along the way. "

Elexis Riley travelled with Wanderers Australia at the end of September, to play in rugby league matches across England. (Supplied: Wanderers Australia)

Elexis hopes to follow in the footsteps of arguably the world's best player, Tamika Upton, who also hails from Rockhampton.

Upton, 27, has risen through the ranks in recent years, first debuting with the Brisbane Broncos in the NRLW in 2019, going on to win five premierships, and now holding the title of captain.

She was awarded the league's top gong in September, making her a three-time Dally M Medal winner.

"I used to go for the Broncos and I still do, but now that I'm in the Cowboys, it's hard," Elexis said with a nervous laugh.

title: Canavan supports Paris Agreement but says EU trade deal goes too far
text:
Nationals leader Matt Canavan says Australia should stay in the Paris Agreement, but has rejected backing a free trade deal with Europe he says will bind the country to net zero.

The Queensland senator, who recently announced his bid for pre-selection for the lower-house seat of Capricornia in central Queensland, said it was important to take measures to reduce emissions where the country could afford it.

"I think we should take measures to reduce emissions over time. It's perfectly reasonable, in a way that doesn't hurt our economy," he said on ABC's Insiders.

"What we can't afford is a mad pursuit of net zero."

The government has set a legislated target to bring down greenhouse gas emissions to net zero by 2050.

Senator Canavan said the EU free trade deal would legally bind Australia to the Paris Agreement, an international climate change treaty, which goes beyond our current commitments.

The provisional text of the deal "includes the obligation to refrain from any act or omission which materially defeats the object and purpose of the Paris Agreement" and that each party shall promote "measures that contribute to the transition to a net zero and low greenhouse gas emission, sustainable circular economy and climate-resilient development".

While Senator Canavan was supportive of Australia staying in the Paris Agreement, he said this was "not what we have signed up to".

"The binding commitments in Paris amount to, having a policy to reduce emissions, taking measures to meet those targets and then reporting against that," he said.

"The purpose and objects [of the Paris Agreement] go further. They include a broad object of carbon neutrality in the second half of the century.

"So what the government is trying to do here is use the EU free trade deal as a backdoor way to bind Australia to net zero."

Senator Canavan added that he wanted to be "constructive" about the free trade deal and has texted Trade Minister Don Farrell to discuss the details.

"He's been talking to me through the media … I texted Don the other day and we'll try and catch up. I'm happy to be constructive," he said.

Senator Farrell has previously said the free trade agreement would yield $10 billion worth of trade and that "there is no renegotiation here".

It is understood the trade deal reaffirms existing climate obligations.

Senator Canavan has repeatedly said his party would not support the agreement in its current form, arguing it is a raw deal for farmers, particularly those in the dairy industry.

"I can't sign off on a deal that wipes out Australian dairy farmers, exposes them to unfair competition, because this deal does not deal with the massive European subsidies that go to dairy — the cheese mountains that result from that — and our dairy industry would be sacrificed," he said.

The Minerals Council has said the deal would benefit companies dealing in critical minerals, which are facing heavy competition from China, by removing tariffs on exports to Europe.

Senator Canavan acknowledged the deal would benefit some industries, but said a local critical minerals company in his region had never mentioned European tariffs, instead saying the carbon tax was a bigger issue.

When asked if he would back a nuclear-powered data centre in the electorate he hopes to one day represent, the Queensland senator said he would welcome it, but the location was always dependent on the will of the local community.

"I'd welcome nuclear power here every day of the week," he said.

"I'd much prefer a nuclear power station next door to me and a 300-metre wind turbine."

The prime minister is due to fly to Türkiye for the UN climate summit COP31 this week.

title: Meet the surgeon saving the careers of cricket's best fast bowlers
text:
Fast, fearsome, and fragile were words often associated with former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond, whose promising cricket career was drastically curtailed by injury.

He debuted as a 26-year-old against Australia in Hobart in 2001, but it was in his next series, against Bangladesh, where he truly announced himself.

He took 11 wickets in two Tests at an average of 13, and it looked like the beginning of a long and lucrative career.

But Bond's back had other ideas. A stress fracture kept him out the game for almost two years from 2003.

Shane Bond is considered "patient zero" after his successful back surgery allowed him to continue his international career. (Phil Walter: Getty Images)

A meeting with back surgeon Grahame Inglis offered him hope he could overcome his injury by undergoing a little-known surgery that is now commonplace in the fast bowling fraternity.

"If I can't fix this, then the career is potentially over," Bond said of his decision to undergo pars stabilisation surgery in 2004.

"He [Inglis] talked about a procedure that he had done, one on a New Zealand high jumper and one other athlete.

" He thought that the chances I came back and bowled fast were slim, but ... I was prepared to give it a go. "

While other injuries limited Bond to just 14 more Tests before he retired in 2009, his back didn't trouble him again.

Last surgeon standing

Renowned New Zealand spinal surgeon Rowan Schouten was working with Dr Inglis at the time and said Bond was "patient zero in this whole story."

Bond took 147 ODI wickets, including a stunning hat-trick against Australia at Bellerive Oval in 2007. (AAP Image/Andrew Cornaga)

The success of that surgery laid the groundwork for a procedure that Schouten and his team have now performed on around 30 professional cricketers.

When surgeons in the UK stopped performing the procedure and Dr Inglis retired, Dr Schouten became the world's leading authority on repairing spinal stress fractures in fast bowlers.

Rowan Schouten says pars stabilisation surgery isn't a new procedure, but has recently become popular with cricketers. (Supplied: rowanschouten.co.nz)

"We were kind of left as the last man standing with experience on international fast bowlers and since then it's taken off essentially," he said.

"We're dealing with calls and connections from all around the world, from the UK, India, South Africa, Europe, Bangladesh, everywhere."

Bond still helps fast bowlers who have struggled with back issues and is often approached for advice.

He's coached Jofra Archer, Jason Behrendorff and James Pattinson, who all had the surgery and returned to play at the top level.

What is pars stabilisation surgery?

When a fast bowler is considering spinal surgery, like Australia's Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris did in 2025, it sounds like a drastic step.

Loading Instagram content

But Dr Schouten said the surgery was straightforward and "not that extreme".

It involves grafting the spine to stimulate repair, before putting screws and wires around the injured portion to provide stability.

WA quick Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris hopes to be even faster after surgery After years of back issues, Lance Morris is finally fit and firing, and the West Australian is keen to put his name in the frame for a Test call up once again.

"We've got a few little added components to it that we believe are important ... but it's a pretty standard technique," he said.

The injury, often referred to as a stress fracture, is common across sport and very prevalent in cricket.

Dr Schouten stressed the surgery is not a fusion, and most stress fractures do not need it.

"You need to preserve all that spinal motion that these guys need to be able to bowl full pace," he said.

Cameron Green opted for surgery in 2024, following several stress fractures during his career. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

If a player did opt to go under the knife, the recovery involves a six-to-nine month rehab program.

"Some stress fractures in some players become a recurring theme," Dr Schouten said.

"And then if you do that, if you have that two or three times in a row over multiple seasons, it can really disrupt a career."

title: Khawaja says he has thrown nobody 'under the bus'
text:
Usman Khawaja insists he has not thrown anyone under the bus with his bombshell ball-tampering revelations that have rocked Australian cricket.

One day on from admitting sandpaper had been used in the Test prior to Cape Town 2018 and the entire team was responsible, Khawaja defended the timing of his claims.

In a five-minute long Instagram explanation, Khawaja revealed he had planned to go public with the details days after the incident before the suspended Steve Smith talked him out of it.

Loading Instagram content

He also detailed how he made another attempt to ensure the entire team took the blame for it in 2021, before a public statement from the bowlers denied any knowledge.

But Khawaja said he had made a promise with his childhood friend David Warner to spill the details of the saga post-retirement in his book, believing Warner, Smith and Cameron Bancroft had taken the fall for the entire team.

"I haven't thrown anyone under the bus," Khawaja said.

"The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're not the victims.

"These three guys took the blame for all of us. They're the victims … people telling them that they're cheats, getting nailed by the crowd. Public humiliation."

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith were both put through the ringer. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

Extracts from Khawaja's memoir Sabr, which will be released on Tuesday, detail how an Australian player applied sandpaper to a ball in the change room in the second Test against South Africa at St George's Park in 2018.

When teammates saw how scuffed up one side became, they realised how much it would swing and Khawaja claims Bancroft volunteered to use the substance.

While Khawaja says that was initially only done at the start of sessions when entering the field, the tactic then expanded to on field in the next Test in Cape Town.

Khawaja also alleges in the book that a member of Australia's coaching staff had encouraged Bancroft to ramp up whatever he was doing with the ball, before the West Australian was caught by cameras and eventually umpires.

In the post on Sunday, Khawaja said he would "not deny" that everyone knew, and revealed how he wanted to go public in 2018 once Smith, Warner and Bancroft were suspended.

"I told Smudge [Smith] that I was going to come clean to the media," Khawaja said.

Usman Khawaja says Steve Smith talked him down from going public earlier. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

"I couldn't believe the penalties he got. But Smudge being the man and leader he was, he talked me out of it.

"He wanted to take the blame. I argued with him, but he was having none of it. That's the first time I try to come out."

Khawaja claimed he spoke extensively with then-coach Justin Langer and Todd Greenberg in 2021 about the team taking collective responsibility, with Greenberg then CEO of the players' union before becoming boss of Cricket Australia.

Lehmann claims 'everyone' was ball tampering Darren Lehmann rejects Usman Khawaja's claims the entire Australian camp knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot, but says "everyone around the world" was ball tampering up until that day.

The 39-year-old then said he never felt comfortable talking about it while back in the Australian team from 2022.

But he argued the fact he had held back the book until after Australia's Test return to South Africa last month was proof this was not a money-making venture.

"Call me a chicken or whatever you want. I didn't know how to do it because I was still in the team," Khawaja said.

"I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I'm not in that team anymore. What I say now isn't a reflection of them anymore.

"I stuck up for all cricketers in the past with the ACA [players' union] fighting for what I thought was right. This is no different.

"These three guys deserve justice and I haven't pointed fingers at anyone."

Khawaja has also been critical of Cricket Australia (CA) over its handling of the investigation into Cape Town, and that he was not interviewed.

CA has maintained it is "comfortable" with its findings from 2018 that only Warner, Smith and Bancroft knew of the idea.

Other players including bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon distanced themselves from the incident, insisting they had no knowledge "of a foreign substance" being taken on the field.

title: Extraordinary scenes as fog descends on 'farcical' FA Cup tie
text:
Does a defeat count if nobody saw it?

Altrincham fans may well be wondering that this weekend, after fog descended upon its FA Cup first round tie against Notts County at Moss Lane in Manchester.

League One side Notts County, featuring Australian former Sydney FC striker Luka Smyth, had taken a first half lead before Manchester-based Altrincham, of the fifth-tier National League, hit the front.

A late equaliser for Nottingham-based County, who won the FA Cup back in the 1893/94 season, forced extra time.

However, by that stage a heavy fog had enveloped the entire stadium, meaning extra time and penalties were played in scarcely believable conditions.

It made one slightly pity the commentators.

"I don't want to worry anyone — we can't see those dugouts at the moment because of the mist," Steve Bower said on the BBC in the closing stages of normal time, before fatefully adding that "it's getting heavier".

"We will try our best to let you know who has got the ball."

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard said on the BBC Radio Nottingham call that "We're looking around … no-one knows where the ball is."

"We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

At least he was only supposed to be summarising.

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," his play-by-play caller Adam Hassell said.

The scenes were reminiscent of another famous foggy incident involving legendary Charlton goalkeeper Sam Bartram.

On Christmas Day, 1937, a London pea souper rolled into Stamford Bridge and completely covered the field.

In his autobiography, Bartram recalled seeing "fewer and fewer figures as we attacked steadily" over the course of the match, right up until a policeman appeared on the edge of his penalty area.

"'What on earth are you doing here?' he gasped. 'The game was stopped a quarter of an hour ago. The field's completely empty,'" Bartram wrote.

"When I groped my way to the dressing-room, the rest of the Charlton team, already out of the bath and in their civvies, were convulsed with laughter."

Fortunately, nothing like that happened in Altrincham, with the game eventually going to penalties, which took place in front of the Altrincham fans.

The Notts County fans, 100 or so metres up the other end of the ground, were left to guess what was happening based on the reactions they could hear through the gloom.

The Notts County fans didn't have the greatest view of the shootout … (Supplied)

They weren't the only ones.

"He's put it wide, I think," commentator Adam Summerton said on TNT Sports as Max Sanders stepped up for Notts County.

"It's hard to tell, I'm sorry, but it's so hard to see up here.

"No, it's in. I'm really sorry, it's so hard for us to see up here," he added as the replay was shown on his monitor.

At least Altrincham fans could see if the ball had gone in or not. (Supplied: TNT Sports)

Meanwhile, Notts County's fans started celebrating after a pause of a couple of seconds, presumably because the Altrincham fans were not.

That pattern continued all the way through the shootout, right up until the final spot kick was taken, by "I think it's [Rosaire] Longelo," Summerton said.

He scored, and Notts County was through to the second round.

At least, I suppose, nobody could see the Altrincham players' disappointment.

Don't worry Eddy Jones, I think most people couldn't see your penalty miss. (Getty Images: Jess Hornby)

title: Spectacular cave site 'neglected' after five years closed to tourists
text:
The reopening of the Princess Margaret Rose Cave has been pushed back yet again.

Public tours of the popular site, 2 kilometres east of the South Australian border, started in the 1940s but stopped in 2021 when the operators retired amid COVID-era travel restrictions.

Today, the spectacular site named after the sister of Queen Elizabeth II is not exactly fit for a royal visit.

"They've had to put gates on to stop the vandalism,” local tourism operator David Graham said.

David Graham said the site was not past the point of no return. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

The cave entrance is within the “dilapidated” visitor centre which Mr Graham recently entered with little difficulty, after he stuck his finger through a hole left by a missing doorhandle next to a cracked window.

"If it keeps going the way it's going … it'll just be vandalised to the point where they'll never re-open it," he said.

The door has since been locked, but Mr Graham said the absence of a permanent occupant at the nearby residence made the location a target.

Elsewhere on the site, there were shards of broken mirror, ripped floors and a large hole inside a shower near the campground and cabins.

A tour of the Princess Margaret Rose site in 2017 (Supplied: Ghurunchi)

Local Liberal MP Roma Britnell said it was disappointing for the community.

"It's just been left to fall into disrepair and neglect,” Ms Britnell said.

Cautious optimism, another delay

The Victorian taxpayer is earmarked to pay $2,135,000 for work at the Princess Margaret Rose Cave site, including new toilets, and upgrades to the wastewater infrastructure and visitor area.

Parks Victoria said work was complete on new cave lighting, handrails, improvements to the steps, and upgrades to electrical systems.

“We know how important the caves are to local tourism, and we’re getting on with the work to reopen them,” a Victorian government spokesperson said in a statement.

Mr Graham said the latest works were a "promising sign" the cave is going to reopen one day.

The foundation for a new toilet block, a short walk from the cave. (ABC News)

In October, a large sign went up near the car park with information about the upgrades.

“Completion: December 2026,” the text on the sign reads.

Parks Victoria’s website was also updated last month with new details about the project timeline.

“Unforeseen contractor availability constraints affected project scheduling, resulting in a revised time frame for construction works,” the website reads.

The government agency now expected the site to re-open in late 2027.

David Graham runs a cabin and boat hire business in the nearby riverside town of Nelson. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

Mr Graham said the re-opening date had been repeatedly delayed.

" It keeps getting pushed back — another 12 months, another 12 months "

Mr Graham, a member of the Nelson Tourism Association, said the continued closure was hurting the local economy.

"It [the cave] contributes to everyone in the area being profitable," he said.

Once a drawcard, still a drawcard

Local fisherman Kym Muller has visited the cave site off the Glenelg River many times since childhood.

Fisherman Kym Muller hopes the cave will reopen soon. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

He said there were "magnificent" lights inside to highlight stalagmites and stalactites.

"It was a very, very pretty cave when it was open, so a lot of tourists came through here," he said.

" Hopefully they do get it up and going again "

While the cave has been closed for more than five years, frustrated holiday-makers have been relatively common in the car park.

Gerry Anthony and Vicki McRae said road signage should make the closure clearer to prevent disappointment. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

"To get right to the front entrance and find that it's just not open is disappointing," traveller Gerry Anthony, who towed a caravan to the closed site, said.

Mr Graham said it was "hard to say" whether there was enough signage.



"[Locals] drive and we see the signs often enough …that's not to say that people do know it's closed," he said.

title: Riding school to close after teaching thousands of students over 50 years
text:
Jenny Haines has tried to count how many people she has taught to ride at the Ranchlands Equestrian Centre over the past 50 years. Somewhere in the thousands, she lost track.

Now, after five decades running the Townsville school, she's closing the gates on Queensland's longest-running riding school under a single owner.

"I think we're up to the eighth third-generation [student] and dozens of second-generation [students]. So it's just so special," Ms Haines said.

Jenny Haines has been running Ranchlands riding school for 50 years. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

When Ms Haines and her husband, Lew, announced they would retire, the community's response was beyond what they anticipated.

The school's final riding lessons will be at the end of the month, after which the Haines plan to travel around Australia in a caravan.

The horses choose the people

A chance encounter about a decade ago gave Ms Haines a new appreciation of the animals she has spent her life teaching people to ride.

Brenda Tanner arrived at Ranchlands looking for a place to run a five-day equine-assisted learning program for a group of veterans.

Doubtful about what Ms Tanner proposed, Ms Haines agreed to lend her property and horses.

Ranchlands will shut later this month. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

"She said, 'Well, the horses pick the people,' so straight away I thought, 'This is ridiculous. I don't believe it,'" she said.

The veterans entered the arena while Ms Haines watched.

"I was hiding behind a tree with my arms folded, feeling very cocky. But gradually, as I watched, the horses do pick the people," she said.

"After 20 minutes, every single client had bonded with a horse," Ms Tanner said.

There was no riding involved. The veterans spent time with the horses on the ground, observing them, grooming them while considering what their own response to the animals might tell them.

"I had always had a feeling that there was more to them, but I was in such a rush to ride them and make them jump jumps and do dancing steps in dressage … I never took the time," Ms Haines said.

"Since I've stopped and lingered longer, as I call it, I've seen things."

Ms Tanner said the Haines made the veterans feel welcome.

"She [Ms Haines] talks in a really connecting way with people and leaves them feeling as though they've been seen. Like she's really seen them," she said.

More than riding lessons

Theresa Robertson, who rode at Ranchlands in the 80s and has since returned as a teacher, has experienced arriving feeling sceptical and leaving with a different view on horses.

"She'll either prove me right or prove me wrong," she recalled thinking.

Theresa Robertson was emotional while talking about what Ranchlands meant to her. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

What stayed with Ms Robertson was a quiet moment holding a long rope attached to a horse, the pair standing still.

"Even though we're not moving forward, we weren't moving backwards, we were standing in the moment," she said.

Ms Robertson said those lessons shaped her teaching in the riding arena.

"They [students] think they're coming to learn to ride a horse, but what they get out of that is tenfold. The horse riding is just a bonus," she said.

When Ms Haines told her Ranchlands was closing, Ms Robertson thought she was joking.

"I was devastated. It's a big part of our world," she said.

The Haines's retirement will end the daily work that has ordered their lives for half a century.

"This has been a whole lifestyle," Ms Haines said.

It's not just a job; it's been a whole life."

title: 'I'm going to marry that guy': Meeting the love of your life at school pick-up
text:
Casey Beros was collecting the child of a family she was nannying for when teacher Ryan Gowland popped his head in her car window. She drove away thinking, "I'm going to marry that guy." And she did.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

Casey: I had been to yoga. I was hot and sweaty and not feeling ready to meet the love of my life.

I pulled into the car line to pick up the child from school, but couldn't spot him.

I saw this very handsome teacher, and he stuck his head in my window.

Ryan: I knew this child's family and car well, so popped my head in to say hello to the mum before quickly realising it wasn't her.

I just remember thinking, "My God, who is this?"

I was pretty sure this child had hitched a ride home with a friend, but we exchanged numbers just in case.

Casey: As I was driving home, Ryan called to let me know the child had indeed hopped a lift home with a friend, and I remember the feeling of not wanting to get off the phone. I thought to myself, "I am going to marry that guy."

'We both had our cab lights on'

Casey, 42, and Ryan, 46 have been together for 12 years.

Casey: We were both ready to meet someone. I always think about that scene in Sex and the City where they are talking about being cabs driving around with their lights on or off. It felt like that.

Ryan felt like home immediately. There was no second guessing. No being unsure of his intentions or how he felt about me.

The mother of the children I was nannying for told me that when it comes to who you marry, you want someone who puts toothpaste on your toothbrush and hands it to you for no reason.

No a word of a lie, a week later Ryan did that.

Ryan: I had actually asked that mum if she knew anyone that was free and nice and interested in going on a date. She said, "There's Casey, but she'll probably eat you alive."

But it happened on its own accord, and very quickly, we never wanted to leave each other.

That family is still in our life, too. The parents emceed our wedding and we adore them.

'We encourage each other to pursue our passions'

Casey and Ryan say being one another's cheerleader is their favourite thing about the relationship. (Supplied)

Casey: Our biggest strength is that we are as generous as we can possibly be with each other.

If I say to him, "I really want to do this course or really want to go to Sydney to see this mentor speak at an event", the answer is always an immediate yes.

If he said to me, "I would really love to go and catch up with my brother for a few days and play golf", not only is my answer yes, I push him to book it and get it done. No matter how inconvenient the timing is.

We are really cheerleading for each other to do that. I love that about our relationship.

Ryan: We are always looking for ways to make each day easier for one another. Having kids is a full-time job.

We just try to make our days as smooth as possible and care for each other in that way.

'We've been through a lot together'

Casey: We've been through more life in the last 10 years than many couples would experience in double the time.

Ryan lost his mum back in 2019 after very quick and rapid deterioration from glioblastoma, a brain tumour.

It was about six weeks from when she got diagnosed until we farewelled her.

I remember at the time she was in Canberra, we were in Sydney, and I was pregnant with a toddler in tow. Ryan just needed to be in Canberra and be with his mum, so that's what we did.

We had a couple of other hits and losses in between that, but the next big one came in June 2021 when I got a call from my dad [in Western Australia] saying he had been diagnosed with mesothelioma — cancer from exposure to asbestos.

At the time, we were in Wagga Wagga celebrating Ryan graduating from his master's degree.

I've got this photo of the four of us — me, Ryan and our two little girls — and we're so happy and he's in his gown and cap.

I look at the picture and all I can think is, "That's the day I got the call."

Casey and Ryan moved to Perth from Sydney when Casey's late father become unwell. (Supplied)

We basically drove from Wagga back to Sydney, then got on a plane. And then WA closed the borders indefinitely due to COVID-19.

We had inadvertently moved back to Perth. We had no goodbyes in Sydney and two suitcases between the four of us. We left the apartment with dirty clothes in the wash basket, assuming we were coming back.

We had Ryan's brother and handful of dear friends pack up our entire apartment over FaceTime, with us saying "Keep that, chuck that, box that."

Ryan: I then had to decide whether to resign from my job of 12 years as deputy principal at a boys' school, or come back to Sydney.

It wasn't a tough choice. I knew I had to stay in Perth with my family.

Casey: Dad passed away in November 2023 and it was Ryan having had that experience with his mum that he was able to be an incredible support to me while I was going through that.

I almost had a blueprint of "I can survive this". His mum was his person, and Dad was mine.

What we love most about each other

Casey and Ryan say they are one another's biggest cheerleaders. (Supplied)

Ryan: Casey constantly keeps me guessing. I never know what is going to happen in our life.

She's got a real zest for life and adventure and fun.

Casey: Ryan is the most consistent person I have ever met. A rock-solid person.

You always get kindness, generosity of spirit, a good mood.

He's like human sunshine and it's such a joy to be around.

title: Socceroos wary of Jordan friendly due to security threats
text:
Football Australia will continue to assess security ahead of the Socceroos' planned friendly against Jordan, with an under-strength squad named amid player concerns over safety.

Tony Popovic's squad was revealed at 10:30pm on Saturday night for upcoming friendlies against Qatar in Doha on November 13 (November 14 AEDT) and Jordan in Amman three days later.

The friendlies were initially meant to serve as preparation for the Asian Cup which has since been pushed back from January to December 2027 due to security concerns in host country Saudi Arabia.

Professional Footballers Australia (the PFA) on Friday said players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

Captain Maty Ryan and fellow veterans Jackson Irvine and Milos Degenek, plus midfielder Aiden O'Neill, are the most prominent omissions from coach Tony Popovic's squad, which includes seven uncapped players.

It is unclear whether those players made themselves unavailable for safety reasons.

As yet, there has been no movement on the Amman fixture, despite Indonesia recently cancelling their own planned friendly in Jordan.

"For the match against Jordan, we will continue to assess the security environment and provide players and staff with timely, comprehensive updates, including relevant safety advice and risk assessments," FA chief executive Martin Kugeler said.

"The safety and wellbeing of our players and staff remains our highest priority."

There are eight changes to the squad from September's friendlies against Brazil in Australia.

Diesel Herrington is one of seven new faces in the Socceroos squad. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

New call-ups are Central Coast defender Diesel Herrington, older brother of Hull City ace Lucas Herrington, Portsmouth striker Thomas Waddingham and FC St. Pauli midfielder Sam Klein.

Attacker Daniel Arzani returns after finding form at Ferencvaros, along with defender Gianni Stensness (Viking FK), who scored against Bayern Munich in the Champions League.

Striker Kusini Yengi joins brother Tete, while goalkeepers Joe Gauci (Lincoln City) and Tom Glover (RB Omiya Ardija) have been recalled.

"While the Asian Cup has been rescheduled, that does not take away from the importance of this window," Popovic said in a statement.

"We have limited opportunities to be together as a group, so every camp and every game is important.

"We will have an eye on continuing to evolve the squad for the future, with our World Cup 2030 qualifying campaign and the Asian Cup both now in the second half of 2027.

"This camp gives us another chance to work with new players and see how they fit into what we are building."

title: Why doctors are writing medical scripts for fresh air
text:

When three-time cancer survivor Sarina Sorrenti and her husband, Sam Pitruzzello, visit their GP, they don’t just leave with scripts for pharmaceutical medications – their doctor also prescribes nature. “Nature walking,” GP Vicki Kotsirilos wrote on a recent script for Sorrenti, alongside a list of vitamins. Sarina Sorrenti and Sam Pitruzzello are among a growing number of Australians benefiting from “nature dosing”. Justin McManus The pair follow the doctor’s orders faithfully, regularly walking beneath the towering gums that line the banks of a billabong near their home in Melbourne’s north. “It’s about absorbing and noticing all the details, everything from the bark on the tree trunk, to the branches, even the leaves,” says Pitruzzello, who has a rare medical condition called myositis, which leads to muscle weakness and pain. “It’s not just ‘go for a walk for exercise’ – now it’s time to heal.”

Advertisement

For the first time, the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) has endorsed new guidelines for prescribing nature. Related Article Science A nature prescription could be just what the doctor ordered Developed by the not-for-profit People and Parks Foundation, the Nature Dose resource details how GPs can prescribe the outdoors for patients as part of their routine care. More intentional than simply being in nature, the practice requires people to make a point of tuning in to sights, sounds, smells and textures. This might include walking near water, feeling the texture of bark or listening to the sound of insects and birds. The guidelines state as little as 20 minutes a day, or two hours a week, can reduce stress, improve mood and wellbeing, enhance sleep and reduce blood pressure. Nature dosing is offered to patients in addition to traditional medical treatment, and is always individualised. People and Parks director Alison Hill says “intergenerational indoorsness” has led to a situation where many people no longer experience the benefits of nature.

Advertisement

She believes this disconnect from nature is fuelling existential crises like climate change, and leading to poor mental health and chronic diseases. “Part of the solution is helping people reconnect with nature and remember that they are part of [it],” she says. “This helps them realise that when we are caring for nature, we are also caring for ourselves now and into the future.” People and Parks director Alison Hill While a growing body of evidence supports the movement, many of the sample sizes are small and rely on self-reporting. A recent UK study of 171 participants found nature prescribing significantly improved wellbeing while reducing symptoms of anxiety and depression.

Advertisement

In Australia, a study of 39 young people with mild to moderate mental health issues found two hours of weekly nature dosing improved their wellbeing, easing psychological distress and significantly reducing loneliness. The participants, who lived in the Shepparton area in northern Victoria, went on bushwalks and engaged in nature journaling, yoga, tree planting and nature photography. A larger UK study of almost 20,000 participants found spending at least two hours a week in nature was linked to significantly greater self-reported health and wellbeing. Advocates have several theories about why nature dosing works. It could provide an escape from the stresses of modern living, or diversify the body’s microbiome through exposure to different bacteria and fungi. Or perhaps, our bodies are simply designed to thrive in the natural world.

Advertisement

Dr Kuljit Singh, the national chair of the RACGP’s social prescribing specific interests group, says while anyone can spend time in nature, a formal nudge, as well as guidance from a doctor, can make all the difference. “It’s empowering,” the Gold Coast-based GP says. “The doctor is telling you to do this, and you are doing it to prevent illness. It gives patients an alternative to a prescription, or a powerful adjunct to one.” Dr Kuljit Singh, the national chair of the RACGP’s social prescribing specific interests group. Singh, who has been prescribing nature to her patients for about 20 years, says the practice is transformative. “It makes a huge difference, from children right through to our seniors,” she says. “For children who have erratic behaviour, panic attacks, or anxiety, spending time looking, listening, and feeling nature really calms them.”

Advertisement

While more than 1000 GPs already prescribe nature to their patients, Singh says the RACGP’s endorsement of the new guidelines will encourage more to follow suit. “When we qualify as doctors, we are always taught to look at lifestyle measures first before we reach for a pill,” she says. “It hasn’t always been given enough weight.” Nature dosing has already been used as part of trials for cancer patients at Alfred Health’s Paula Fox Melanoma and Cancer Centre and at headspace in Shepparton. As part of another study, new parents in the City of Banyule in Melbourne’s north-east were prescribed group-based nature dosing to reduce their risk of loneliness. Vicki Kotsirilos says prescribing nature is a no-brainer. “There is surprisingly lots of evidence demonstrating regular exposure to nature is beneficial to human health physically, mentally, emotionally and spiritually,” she says.

Advertisement

“Nature contact can improve sleep and mental health, reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety, ADHD, reduce aggression, and brings greater happiness, wellbeing, life satisfaction and social connectedness.” The shift has been profound for Sorrenti and Pitruzzello. Pitruzzello and Sorrenti say nature dosing has transformed their health and wellbeing. Justin McManus As frogs croak in the billabong and dragonflies skim the water’s murky surface, Sorrenti says her nervous system is now back in balance. She feels more energised than she did in her 20s and 30s. Her mental health, which took a battering following three separate cancer diagnoses, has also improved. As well as daily walks in nature, Sorrenti stands barefoot in her garden for 15 minutes every morning.

Advertisement

“People just want to go to doctors and ask them to fix them,” she says. “You have to be part of the healing.” For Pitruzzello, regular nature dosing has improved his motivation to stay fit and healthy. It’s also helped him come to terms with having a chronic health condition. “When you have chronic conditions like mine, it affects your mental health,” he says. “You can just get into this spiral ... you want to make sure that you live with it the best you can.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. The residents of Martha Cove are used to paying a premium for their picturesque marina lifestyle. The development in Safety Beach on the Mornington Peninsula is home to about 3000 people who live in properties ranging from apartments to luxury villas. Collectively, they fund the maintenance of boardwalks, underpass lifts, harbour dredging and other features of the area even though the public has right of access. The Martha Cove residential development offers a waterfront lifestyle, but residents pay for the upkeep. Joe Armao But now residents are in a dispute with the Victorian Department of Transport and Planning over its plans to charge them a combined $541,000 to update lights in a public underpass used by motorists daily. Martha Cove Owners Corporation chairman Neil Pope, a former Victorian Labor government minister, said a dated agreement between the developer of Martha Cove, Mornington Peninsula Shire and the department had resulted in residents being saddled with the cost of maintaining public infrastructure.

Advertisement

“This is ultimately an issue of fairness, accountability and the proper use of property owners’ money,” he said. Construction began on the Martha Cove development in 2004, and it was built progressively over the following years. The area now has more than 1800 dwellings and about 830 marina berths for boats. Neil Pope driving in the underpass where the lights will be upgraded. Joe Armao Pope said residents understood they faced additional costs to live in the area, with its associated waterfront access. Last year, residents spent a combined $450,000 on underpass lifts, which are open to the public, as well as replacing a 2.3-kilometre timber boardwalk with fibreglass resin polymer after it became slippery and dangerous. But Pope said it was outrageous the Department of Transport and Planning wanted residents to fund the upgrade of 50 lights in an 80-metre stretch of underpass. The department wants to upgrade the current sodium vapour and fluorescent lights with LED.

Advertisement

“We accept that we have to look after the marina,” Pope said. “But it just makes it darn hard when we have to budget for stuff we don’t believe we should have to pay the full amount for.” Pope served as the state MP for Monbulk from 1982 to 1992. Under the Cain and Kirner governments, he served as the minister for labour, minister for school education and minister for youth affairs. Now he is frustrated with the bureaucracy on his side of politics, and said the department had failed to adequately explain how it reached the figure of $541,000, and hadn’t provided residents with design documents. He also expressed concern about the potentially enormous future costs of maintaining the underpass. “This [cost] is an extraordinary development and one that has caused considerable concern among residents,” he said.

Advertisement

Under a section 173 agreement, which sets out long-term obligations for property owners, residents at Martha Cove are required to fund maintenance and replacements in the area. The light replacement project is due to begin this month. Residents are required to contribute to a sinking fund, which covers infrastructure and maintenance in the marina. With the department able to access that fund, Pope said residents could not stop the department from extracting the money. A bus emerging from the underpass where the lights will be upgraded. Joe Armao Pope said the Martha Cove waterway had fundamentally changed the area, by creating a boating activity destination with access to Port Phillip Bay. A spokesperson for the Department of Transport and Planning said it was working closely with the Martha Cove Owners Corporation to ensure the underpass was maintained in accordance with safety standards.

Advertisement

“As a privately funded development, the owners corporation is responsible for the ongoing operation and maintenance of the Martha Cove underpass,” the spokesperson said. The department said the underpass was built in 2005 to facilitate the lowering of Marina Drive beneath the entrance channel to Martha Cove Marina. Pope says it’s unfair for residents to pay for new lighting in the underpass. Joe Armao The department said the light replacement program addressed performance and reliability issues and complied with the department’s procurement policy. The department also said it had providing briefings and shared information with residents since the project development phase began two years ago. But Liberal MP Anthony Marsh, whose seat of Nepean covers the marina, lashed the department’s handling of the project.

Marsh said the owners corporation supported replacing ageing lights, but did not accept the “extraordinary bill” without proper scrutiny of the project’s scope and costs. “Martha Cove residents should not be left carrying an unreasonable and avoidable financial burden,” he said. text:

Updated PoliticsFederalDefence Victoria Barracks sale abandoned following backlash Eryk Bagshaw and Harriet Alexander Updated November 8, 2026 — 4:22pm ,first published November 8, 2026 — 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Albanese government has bowed to public pressure and abandoned the sale of Victoria Barracks, removing its most high-profile defence asset from its attempt to claw back $3 billion in taxpayer money. The decision, announced on Sunday, means the 186-year-old Victoria Barracks in Paddington will remain in government hands. Loading The government has also reversed course on selling land containing an ancient Angophora red gum forest inside HMAS Penguin on Sydney Harbour, which will now be handed over to the Sydney Harbour Federation Trust. Victoria Barracks, the colonial-era sandstone military headquarters, will not be sold, but it will also no longer be used as an active Australian Defence Force facility. Instead, it will be opened to the public and the space will be commercialised to fund the maintenance of the building. Part of the site may also be developed.

Advertisement

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had lived in Sydney his whole life and Sunday’s announcement was the first time he had stepped foot inside Victoria Barracks. “This is an asset for Sydney that should be opened up for Sydneysiders,” he said. “Most Sydneysiders have not been to this beautiful site.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Deputy Prime Minster Richard Marles at Victoria Barracks on Sunday. George Chan The move now opens the door to further challenges to the government’s plans to sell off more than 60 other sites around the country. The Headland Preservation Group, which has been protesting plans to sell part of HMAS Penguin at Balmoral on Sydney Harbour, said the decision to hand over the forest to the Sydney Harbour Foreshore Trust while retaining the site’s physical structures and beach for the defence force was a great result.

Advertisement

“It’s the outcome we’ve been advocating for, which is terrific,” said Jill L’Estrange, president of the Headland Preservation Group. “The Sydney Harbour Foreshore Trust is next door – it already manages a large part of the forest and this is another segment of it so it’s really appropriate. They won’t be making any money out of it on this basis, but Albanese had always said that this harbour foreshore needed to be protected so he’s staying true to his word.” An aerial view of the HMAS Penguin naval base at Middle Head. Alamy Marles had until September maintained that Victoria Barracks would be sold, describing it as “the oldest wine cellar in Sydney” used by only a section of the military elite. The comments provoked a backlash from supporters of the site and galvanised the Save Victoria Barracks Alliance. An unlikely coalition of veterans’ groups, former prime ministers Paul Keating, John Howard and Tony Abbott, Premier Chris Minns and federal, state and local politicians all spoke out against the sale of the site.

Advertisement

The Daily Telegraph, which first reported the Albanese government’s backflip on Sunday morning, also campaigned heavily against the sale. Albanese said on Sunday afternoon there were limits on what could be done at the site due to the heritage listing, and the decision to keep it in public hands ensured there would be no interference that would downgrade its heritage significance. He did not rule out the possibility that parts of the site may be put out on a 99-year lease. Politicians including Allegra Spender, Alex Greenwich, John Howard and Tony Abbott joined the Victoria Barracks protest. Oscar Colman “What we’re open to is making sure that there’s proper use of the site, it’s respected, and in terms of commercial opportunities that are there, they’ll be explored,” he said. The government announced three other Defence sites, including Victoria Barracks and Point Cook in Melbourne and Fort Queenscliff near Geelong, would remain publicly owned and opened up for community access.

Advertisement

Marles said the government remained committed to moving Defence personnel off the four sites within two years, and the Australian War Memorial would be commissioned to “interpret” the sites and tell their stories. “In respect of the stories which relate to defence, which are captured in these buildings, those stories will be told in a bigger and better way to a much larger audience, which is a much better heritage outcome,” Marles said. “We need to have a defence force that is focused. Every person who wears our nation’s uniform matters. Every hour they spend counts, and every dollar which resources them is precious. Which is why we are making these decisions.” Loading NSW Premier Chris Minns said stopping the sale was the right decision.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Planning The price of Victoria Barracks is much higher than $200 million Nadia Teong Clinical psychologist “I’m glad they’ve made this call, and I congratulate them for it,” he said. “I think [the heritage] would have been lost if it was sold off to a private developer.” The government estimated maintaining the site as a defence facility would cost $200 million over the next 10 years. But stopping the sale of Victoria Barracks will still punch a hole worth hundreds of millions of dollars in the government’s attempt to recoup $3 billion from ailing defence assets. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said he would fight to keep the sites in Defence hands, as well as HMAS Penguin, Lancer Barracks, and Irwin Barracks. NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane expanded the list to include Randwick Barracks.

Advertisement

“This was never about modernising the Defence estate – it was just another smash and grab for revenue by a Prime Minister who can’t manage money and can’t control his spending,” Taylor said in a statement on X. City of Sydney councillor Zann Maxwell, who has campaigned for Victoria Barracks to be part of the solution to housing supply shortages in inner suburbs, said the government’s new position was consistent with everything the community wanted. Related Article Defence Marles wants Defence out of $3 billion sites ‘as soon as possible’ This included public ownership, public access, provision of housing and for the historic buildings to be repurposed for civic, cultural and appropriate commercial activities. “Those who argued the site should remain a closed-off military base for the exclusive use of a small part of the army still won’t be happy, but this is the right call,” Maxwell said.
