A young couple paid $4.25 million for an eye-catching mid-century modern house in Clontarf, in a hard-fought Saturday auction that defied Sydney’s weak property market. The five-bedroom house at 26 Cutler Road featured timber beams, exposed brick interiors, a fireplace, a cantilevered concrete slab and views over Middle Harbour. The property was one of 964 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 49 per cent from 571 reported results throughout the week, while 222 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. It was the first test of the market’s reaction to the Reserve Bank’s fifth cash rate hike for the year on Tuesday, to 4.85 per cent. Although the clearance rate remains at weak levels, it was a similar result to last week’s early read of 48 per cent, as many buyers already in the market may have factored the rate rise into their budgets.

Eight parties registered for the Clontarf home. Bidding began at $3.55 million, below the price guide of $3.9 million, and rose rapidly at first. The stride later shortened to offers of $5000 to $10,000. The home passed its reserve price of $3,925,000 but selling agent Michael Clarke of Clarke & Humel Property did not have a chance to call the home on the market until the bidding reached $4 million. The price guide and reserve were set at $4.5 million. title: $2b and plenty of new seats: Inside airlines’ battle for first-class supremacy
text:

BusinessCompaniesAviation $2b and plenty of new seats: Inside airlines’ battle for first-class supremacy Chris Zappone November 8, 2026 — 2:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. With high-paying passengers driving airline profitability, carriers are locked in an escalating race to outshine one another through what they offer in their premium cabins. Singapore Airlines has revealed the seats to be installed in many of its A350s as part of a long-awaited $S2 billion ($2.26 billion) cabin refit – for first class, business class, premium economy and economy. The new cabins will also be in its upcoming order of 31 Boeing 777-9s. The complexity and cost of the cabin refit tells a much broader story about the battle to cater to the premium traveller with better seating, cabins, service and food. That battle is playing out against the constraints of the industry as it struggles to keep up with surging demand for seats. The Singapore Airlines refit was announced in 2024 with expectations the first of 41 A350-900 planes would be ready by this year. Instead, the airline said this year that the first planes would start to be refitted by the first quarter of 2027, the revised timeline reflecting what it said were industry-wide supply chain constraints and a delay in the certification of one of the new seats.

Advertisement

Safety regulators such as the US Federal Aviation Administration certify planes and interiors for flight. Singapore Airlines senior vice president customer experience Yeoh Phee Teik told a press conference on Friday: “Seats have already been certified on the 777-9. As you know, the 777-9 aircraft itself has not yet passed certification.” Loading “You have to understand the intricacies of that; the seats on the A350 have not yet been certified. We are undergoing that process right now.” Which is to say seats for a plane not yet cleared for use are approved, but new seats for a plane already in use (the A350) have not. The company expects them to be approved by 2027.

Advertisement

Singapore Airlines’ Boeing 777-9s are expected by the second half of 2027, said Lee Lik Hsin, chief commercial officer. “We are working hand in hand and working very hard with our partners [the plane and seat makers] to make sure that we achieve those milestones.” Across the industry, planes are awaiting seats, or indeed awaiting certification. The bottlenecks in the production and certification processes exacerbate each other. The unveiling of the business class seats in the RECARO factory in Germany last year. The Age These delays have prompted airlines, constrained in their ability to get new aircraft, to resort to cabin refreshes to stay competitive. Qantas announced one for its 737s in 2025. This has set off a rush in demand for new premium seating, which has strained both the industry producing it, and the few regulators in the US and Europe who can approve it.

Advertisement

Singapore Airlines’ first-class cabins, for example, move away from the sameness, featuring an undulating shape, breaking rigid lines and creating an aisle that is curved, a rare sight on a jet. “The curve in the aisle unlocks more space for the passenger,” said designer Ben Rowan, of London-based PriestmanGoode, who is the mastermind behind the layout. “You’re not looking at office cubicles in a straight line. This is a much more curving, welcoming space.” Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, individual full-flat beds 80 inches in length and 30 inches in width, and adjacent seats that can transform into a two-seater sofa for daytime lounging are all features. The slightly hexagonal cabins allow passengers sleeping on the “lie-flat” beds to turn and place their feet on the floor, creating a sensation similar to a bedroom.

Advertisement

“When you sleep and you get up at home, what’s the first thing you do?” asked Lee, the chief commercial officer. “You turn to the side, and you sit on your bed. We couldn’t do that before. “Today we can, because the curved walls provide a little bit of space for you to put your foot down, and maybe collect yourself before you stand up.” A redesign of a cabin in a style that complements Singapore Airlines’ high service level aims to reinforce its position as a premium airline, one with the fortune of geography to pick up Europe-Asia traffic lost to its rival Gulf airlines when the Iran conflict began in February. The first class seat in full lie flat position, seen at the factory in North Carolina in the US. Chris Zappone Singapore Airlines flights from Australia to Europe gained 25 per cent more passengers in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the same time last year, with fares surging 109 per cent in that time, according to data from aviation data and analytics company Cirium.

Advertisement

Singapore Airlines’ refit itself was announced after it became clear the premium airline wasn’t going to get the 777-9 it ordered on time. Made by Collins Aerospace in the US, the first-class seats are the result of a nearly decade-long process. PriestmanGoode began designs in 2018. The long timeframe is partially because of COVID and partially because of cascading disruptions to manufacturing afterwards. Trying out a mock-up of the first-class seats last year in North Carolina. NIne New premium economy seats will have adjustable foot and leg rests, dedicated storage, and a cocktail tray for drinks.

Advertisement

Economy seats have a redesigned seat-reclining mechanism with better knee and shin clearance, as well as an adjustable headrest. RECARO’s final assembly line for airplane seats. RECARO For all the soothing subtle colours of first class, and the golds and browns Singapore Airlines has been known for, the airline has chosen a blue-grey colour for its new business seats. The business seat, designed by BMW Designworks and made by Germany-based Recaro, reclines into a 79-inch-long fully flat bed, replacing the diagonal set-up Singapore business class is known for. The meal tray, which is often one of the most troublesome necessities of a seat, drops from below the seat back, pulls out and extends.

Advertisement

Yet, the complexity of the seat – and its safety requirements – have further tied up and delayed supply chains which have come under intense strain since COVID, a time when demand initially shuddered to a halt, prompting staff exits, and the closure of parts makers. Editor's pick Updated

Aviation Qantas to raise airfares, cut flights as fuel costs rise by $1 billion Part of the bottleneck for cabins is the number of companies qualified to do the seat design and construction. As AeroDynamic Advisory managing director Richard Aboulafia said at a forum held in June: “There aren’t that many seat suppliers, and it’s a rather labour-intensive operation”. Aboulafia said a kind of groupthink had taken hold in the aviation industry as airlines decided to retrofit their entire fleet. Part of what makes commercial aviation so safe are the standards built into aircraft manufacturing; everything that goes into a plane must be tested and certified for use. That includes seats.

Advertisement

“So the supply challenges and the certification challenges are magnified immensely by these specific industry dynamics in the seating business,” Aboulafia said. With so many different seats designed and produced in the industry, testing requires time. To expedite matters, seat-maker Recaro’s factory in Schwabisch Hall, Germany, has its own crash-test facility. Seat-maker Recaro’s factory in Schwabisch Hall, Germany, conducts tests needed to certify seats. Nine A catapult hurtles a dummy in a seat across a track, while 10 cameras and sensors record the impact. In one violent action, the seat is tested and photographed. At this facility, a single business-class seat can run up to €100,000 ($162,000) for each test. Specific certifications can require up to 18 separate tests. A state-run program aiming to reduce barriers to treatment and accelerate access to ADHD medications has run into immediate issues after a bungled Victorian government website directed patients to the wrong clinics. Premier Ben Carroll last Monday celebrated an easing of the rules that govern who can diagnose ADHD, with 150 newly trained general practitioners across the state now able to diagnose, treat and prescribe stimulants for the neurodevelopmental disorder. About 150 GPs can now diagnose ADHD under changes introduced by the state government, but a directory bungle made it difficult for some to be found. Matt Davidson Previously, only specialists such as paediatricians and psychiatrists could treat ADHD, leading to high costs and waiting lists of up to a year for the estimated 163,000 Victorian children and 320,000 adults living with the condition. But an official Department of Health website that went live on October 26 to direct families to clinics offering the new GP ADHD clinics included at least 15 services that are not accepting patients as part of the program – including one health service that is not even open.

Advertisement

Mental Health Victoria chief executive Phillipa Thomas. A handful of other clinics taking part in the program were missing from the directory, despite their doctors undertaking training from the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) as part of the government’s program. Mental Health Victoria CEO Phillipa Thomas said the confusion meant that non-participating health services were last week inundated with calls from people trying to make appointments for ADHD services that weren’t on offer. “Many callers were already frustrated at having been turned away from other incorrectly listed providers, and understandably people’s patience was pretty thin. You can imagine how the situation compounded over days; with increasingly distressed callers at one end, and increasingly distressed and overwhelmed health service staff at the other,” Thomas said. “It’s a disappointing start and a reminder that it’s not in anyone’s interest for significant policy changes like these to be rushed.”

Advertisement

The incorrectly listed clinics include some that do not offer GP services at all, as well as specialist services such as mental health and emergency units that do not book consultations. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Psychosis linked to ADHD medication on the rise, doctors warn When The Age contacted the department about the directory errors, a government spokesperson confirmed that “a small number of clinics” had requested changes to their listings on the ADHD care in general practice webpage. In the days that followed, 14 services – including clinics in Altona Meadows, Barwon Heads, Frankston, Moe, Port Fairy, and Wodonga – were removed from the list, while five others were added. One service – The Living Room, which provided support in Melbourne’s Hosier Lane for people experiencing homelessness – was only removed from the official list on Friday, despite having closed last month.

Advertisement

Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Victorian Branch Chair, associate professor Simon Stafrace, said it was vital to remove barriers for people to access ADHD care closer to home. “We urge the Victorian government to make sure the information is up-to-date as quickly as possible, so this important reform can be delivered as intended, particularly in communities where people already face significant barriers to accessing ADHD and mental health care,” he said. Loading The government denied that it had bungled the rollout, saying the directory changes included instances where ADHD-trained doctors had consented to the publication of their details before later requesting removals. “A small number of clinics requested changes to their public listings, which have been updated,” a government spokesperson told The Age.

Advertisement

Related Article Mental health Victorian GPs to diagnose ADHD and prescribe medication for it under new reforms The government has now asked the RACGP, which earlier this year oversaw the training of GPs involved in its program, to ensure doctors communicate with their clinics about their participation in the program and their public listing on its directory. RACGP Victoria Chair Dr Anita Muñoz said GP ADHD assessments were a positive step towards improving access, and that patients welcomed the move. “The Victorian Department of Health’s list of participating clinics is regularly updated to reflect local capacity. Clinics may request to be added as services expand, and removed when practices are no longer able to take on new patients,” she said. “The level of demand we’re seeing demonstrates why these reforms matter, and why we really need to train more GPs to improve access to care. Giving more GPs the skills and authority to assess and diagnose ADHD will help patients access care sooner, closer to home.”

Advertisement

Related Article Explainer

Mental health What’s ADHD and why are more adults being diagnosed with it? The Age last week revealed psychiatrists’ concerns that a growing number of patients are developing psychosis, including paranoia and hallucinations, after taking medication to treat ADHD. Rates of ADHD diagnosis have skyrocketed in recent years due to increased awareness of the disorder, leading to a surge in the number of Australians using stimulant medications. In response to rising demand and longer wait times, state governments have been easing restrictions on who can diagnose and treat the condition. In December, Queensland became the first state allowing GPs to diagnose and prescribe for ADHD. Since then, South Australia, NSW, Western Australia and Tasmania have followed suit. Victoria’s changes mean that since October 26, trained GPs can diagnose and treat ADHD in adults and children aged six years and over, in a move that Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said would save families thousands of dollars and up to a year of waiting time for an appointment.

Mark Nawaqanitawase has been with his new club in Japan for just one week, but Saitama Wild Knights attack coach Berrick Barnes says the former Roosters premiership winner is already impressing his new teammates. Nawaqanitawase is expected to make his debut in a pre-season game against Tochigi Honda Heat on December 5, leaving him with just over a month to adjust to a new language and culture. Mark Nawaqanitawase at pre-season training with his new Japanese club Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights Instagram But Barnes, the former Wallabies playmaker who also worked with Nawaqanitawase as an assistant coach with the national team in 2023, has no doubts the star recruit will be an instant success. According to Barnes, Nawaqanitawase’s exploits in rugby league, which also included a State of Origin series win with NSW, are mostly unknown to the Wild Knights’ Japanese squad members, given the small footprint the 13-man code has in the country.

But the winger’s arrival has still created significant excitement at club headquarters, even for a squad used to regularly training with World Cup-winning Springboks Lood de Jager and Damian de Allende. “The Japanese boys don’t even know who he is, that’s the truth” Barnes said. “I mean a couple might, just because of all of us foreigners. Like, you can get the best All Blacks in the world walking through the door and they’ll be just like, ‘Hey mate, how are you going?’ “But there are a few of them who are genuinely nervous and excited to have him [Nawaqanitawase] come in the building. So I don’t see that too often. I’ll say that.”

Nawaqanitawase arrived in Japan at the start of November, but has already impressed with his reintegration into rugby after a two-and-a-half year absence. “You can already see the leadership qualities [he has],” Barnes said. “He’s also got a positivity about him that breeds confidence in others; he genuinely believes not just in his own ability, but that of others and he gives others confidence. Mark Nawaqanitawase won his first NRL title with the Roosters. George Chan “It’s only taken me a couple of days to see that, and it’s such a rare quality. It’s been really refreshing to see.”

After winning 51 Test caps, Barnes played for the Wild Knights from 2013 until 2018. Foreign players in Japanese rugby were rarer when Barnes arrived, and the former Wallaby had to learn enough of the language to survive on and off the field. Today, however, Nawaqanitawase will benefit from most plays being called in English, and having a translator at training. The multicultural squad includes English, Tongan, South African, New Zealand and South Korean imports alongside the Japanese players, some of whom also work for the club’s owners, Panasonic. Berrick Barnes worked under Eddie Jones as an assistant coach with the Wallabies in 2023. Getty The Wild Knights are based in the regional city of Kumagaya, which has a population of under 200,000. The bright lights of Tokyo are just 40 minutes away by bullet train, but the players live in a smaller city that allows them to build their own unique identity.

title: Donald Trump offers UFC chief Dana White job as White House press secretary

In brief Donald Trump invited UFC chief Dana White to be the new White House press secretary in a social media post.

The White House press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia's tenure ended last month.

US President Donald Trump has asked mixed martial arts promoter Dana White to serve as White House press secretary and called on him to bring some fighters along as assistants "even though some are not from our country."

White, chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, is a "violent Fighter and Warrior," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Trump also asked for six current or former UFC titleholders to join White, including two athletes from Russia's Dagestan region, Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov, Americans Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier and "Kayla Harris," likely a reference to Kayla Harrison, and Amanda Nunes, a Brazilian native who became a US citizen last year.

"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote.

White and UFC's parent company, TKO Group Holdings TKO.N, did not immediately return requests for comment. However, CNN reported White has declined the president's invitation.

The White House press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia's tenure ended last month after less than a week. Zacharia replaced Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August.

White and Trump first worked together in the early 2000s, when Trump's Taj Mahal casino hosted some UFC events. But they have become closer allies since the UFC chief publicly backed Trump's presidential campaign in 2016.

In a social media post, Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors," and he praised Wiles for doing "an outstanding job." Trump said the change would take effect on Monday.

A White House official said Miller’s appointment signals that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides.

title: How thousands of 'special votes' will now determine New Zealand's election winner
text:
IN BRIEF The NZ election has ended without a clear winner.

The result could be decided by 700,000 votes and minor party negotiations.

It could be weeks before the winner of New Zealand's general election emerges, with neither of the two major parties securing enough seats to form a government.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party secured 42 seats in the country's parliament, while former Prime Minister Chris Hipkins' centre-left Labour Party won 36 seats.

The National Party, combined with its coalition partners ACT and NZ First, had a projected count of 67 seats, according to the NZ Electoral Commission.

Opposition parties Labour, the Greens and the Māori Party, together with the new force Opportunity — which has not yet said which side it will join in a coalition — combined for 63 seats.

Luxton has said that he is confident in securing another term, while Hipkins has said he will wait for the final results.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Final results in weeks

To control the New Zealand parliament, a party needs a majority of 61 seats out of the baseline 120 seats.

However, under New Zealand's Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) voting system, the total number of seats can increase because of "overhang seats", changing the number needed for a majority. Voters can decide how many seats a party gets during the election.

In the current election, the majority needed to lead is 66 seats, according to the country's public broadcaster, Radio New Zealand (RNZ).

READ MORE New Zealand election still on a knife edge with more than 90 per cent of votes counted

In the party vote, Labour had a majority with a small margin, with 29.36 per cent of the party vote and National securing 29.21 per cent, according to RNZ.

The Greens recorded their best-ever national vote, on 13.30 per cent, as did ACT, on 10.92 per cent, while NZ First was at 9.78 per cent and Opportunity at 5.96 per cent.

The results might also change when an estimated 700,000 'special votes' from out-of-electorate and overseas ballots — which typically favour the left — are added to the mix.

They will all be included on November 27, when the final results are released, meaning it might take weeks to understand who will be in charge of New Zealand's next government.

About 400,000 special votes are yet to be counted, with 96,000 from overseas.

While the final results will be announced in weeks, the current New Zealand prime minister has said he is confident of a second term.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he's confident of another term in government while Labour leader Chris Hipkins says results are still being counted. Source: Getty, AAP / Hagen Hopkins/Ben McKay

'Time to sit tight'

Luxon said his Nationals party had secured the most seats, giving them a mandate to form government.

"Ultimately, New Zealanders have given us the biggest seats in parliament 42 seats as it stands today and a pathway to form a government."

But he said his party and all New Zealanders now needed to wait for the final results on 27 November.

If he does secure another term, it could be without important figures in the election: Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Defence Minister Paul Goldsmith and Speaker Gerry Brownlee, who all conceded their races, while Transport Minister Chris Bishop is also a likely loser.

"Some of the hardest phone calls tonight have been to colleagues and friends who look unlikely to make it back into parliament," Luxon said.

Meanwhile, Labour leader Chris Hipkins said on Saturday that he will wait for the final results.

"As things stand tonight, it's clear we're not going to know the exact shape of the next government for a little while longer yet," he said.

"When the final result is known, I'll have quite a bit more to say."

The results have followed weeks of election campaigns dominated by cost-of-living issues and the economy, with the country's unemployment rate at its highest in a decade.

The war in the Middle East and the resulting global fuel shock have been widely blamed for the damage to New Zealand's trade-dependent economy.

The outsider who could decide next government

Support for Labour and National has fallen to historically low levels. Surveys suggest voters have lost faith in the major parties' ability to revive the sluggish economy and make the changes needed to repair ageing infrastructure.

If the National-led coalition loses its majority at the official count, either it or a left-leaning coalition would require the support of the centrist Opportunity Party, which looks likely to enter parliament for the first time.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said she would look to negotiate with the party that secured the largest number of seats after the official results.

Wong has said she would look to negotiate with the party that secures the most seats in parliament and that it would be possible to find common ground with National or Labour.

Qiulae Wong has been a politician for less than a year, but the 38-year-old could hold the balance of power in New Zealand's parliament Credit: Jonathan Killick/Stuff via AP

Wong, a former sustainable-business consultant, answered an advertisement for the role of head of the decade-old party and took over in November 2025.

She quickly oversaw a rebrand and a dramatic rise in Opportunity's popularity.

The party's flagship policies centre on tax: An annual NZ$19,400 (A$$15,685) universal basic income for most New Zealand residents funded by a 1.75 per cent annual land tax. The party also wants to simplify the country's income tax system.

National and Labour have both ruled out adopting Opportunity's tax policies.

"It might seem like we've just arrived, that this is an overnight success, but to many in this room, this result has been a long time coming," Wong told cheering supporters in Auckland on Saturday night.

title: The little-known migration story behind one of Australia's biggest Diwali celebrations
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

For the first Punjabi Sikh families who settled in Woolgoolga, Diwali was a reminder of home, of the traditions, language and familiar rituals they had left behind in India.

Far from their families and the celebrations they had grown up with, they marked the festival of lights, which celebrates the triumph of good over evil, quietly in their homes. There were no community gatherings or public festivities, just families finding small ways to keep a piece of home alive in a new country.

Deesha Maan was among the children who grew up between these two worlds.

Deesha Maan (left) arrived in Woolgoolga in 1964, but her family's ties to Australia stretch back to 1901, when her grandfather arrived in Cairns, Queensland, to work on a farm. Credit: Supplied

Just seven when she arrived in Woolgoolga in 1964, Maan remembers trading a childhood in a three-storey house in Punjab, northern India, for a life on the gravel roads and banana farms of a small coastal town, 550km north of Sydney, where she struggled to understand the language around her.

Deesha Maan (bottom right) says she is teaching her grandkids about the same traditions that her mum taught her, but in English. Credit: SBS Punjabi

For the town's Sikh community, Diwali is also observed as Bandi Chhor Divas, commemorating the release of the sixth Sikh Guru, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, who had been imprisoned because of his faith. When Mughal emperor Jahangir granted Guru permission to leave prison, he refused to go unless the other prisoners were freed too.

The evolution of these celebrations reflects a broader story of Punjabi Sikh migration to Australia, and the generations who have built lives here while keeping their cultural and religious traditions alive.

Woolgoolga's Sikh roots

Woopie, as locals fondly call the town, is home to Australia's first Sikh gurdwara, a place of worship. Opened in June 1968, the gurdwara on Hastings Street is now listed on the NSW State Heritage Register, recognising its significance to the history of Sikh settlement in Australia.

The original gurdwara (Sikh place of worship), opened in 1968 and now heritage-listed, stands beside a new three-storey gurdwara completed in 2019. Credit: SBS Punjabi

The town's local museum traces the community's history to six pioneering Punjabi Sikh families who established themselves by the early 1950s, after Punjabi migrants arrived in the 1940s.

Some early settlers travelled on British passports, reflecting their status as British subjects under India's colonial system.

Image of the six early Punjabi settlers displayed at the town's local museum titled 'The forefathers'. Credit: SBS Punjabi

The community grew over subsequent decades, with many early migrants initially working as labourers on banana farms before moving into farming themselves.

The 2021 Census recorded 6,151 people living in Woolgoolga, of whom 1,059 identified Sikhism as their religion — over 17 per cent of the population. At least 1,000 residents reported speaking Punjabi at home.

A local road has also been named after Arkan, the surname of one of Woolgoolga's pioneering Sikh families, who went on to establish the region's second gurdwara.

Maan says the two gurdwaras in Woolgoolga serve not only the Sikh community but also welcome people from other cultural and religious backgrounds. This spirit of inclusiveness dates back to the establishment of the first gurdwara, whose inaugural management committee included three non-Sikh members of European heritage.

The inaugural committee of the first gurdwara (Sikh place of worship) also included non-Sikh members of European heritage. Credit: SBS Punjabi

"We were in fact encouraged by the Australians of European backgrounds to build this first gurdwara premises," Maan says.

Woolgoolga's Sikh farming legacy

As the news of the first-ever gurdwara in Australia spread, the Sikhs from other parts of the country began visiting Woolgoolga. Some, like Bhupinder Singh Lally, eventually decided to settle there.

Bhupinder Singh Lally's family was among the first to buy land in Woolgoolga, where they once grew bananas and now run blueberry farms. Credit: SBS Punjabi

"I remember visiting the gurdwara for the first time with my father on Christmas Day in 1968," Lally tells SBS Punjabi, recalling a moment that brought together his family's Sikh heritage and their growing connection to Australia.

Lally's grandfather and father had worked and lived in Gordonvale, Queensland. His own sons now run blueberry farms in Woolgoolga, reflecting the changing generations and agricultural livelihoods within the community. He says when his family first arrived, Indian migrants had limited opportunities to own land, making the transition from farm labour to farm ownership a significant step for many.

Despite working alongside people from different backgrounds, social acceptance took time. Lally says over time, Woolgoolga's Sikh community became a visible part of local life, with festivals such as Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas gaining wider recognition.

"Until then, we used to celebrate important events by praying under the tents," Lally says.

"Now, Diwali celebrations are at a much larger scale. Hindus, Nepali, Punjabis, we all celebrate together."

But what makes these occasions particularly special, Lally says, is the way Punjabi traditions have blended with the Australian way of life.

It is a sentiment echoed by others in the community.

Satpal Singh is a descendant of a pioneering Punjabi Sikh family that settled in Woolgoolga in the 1940s. Credit: SBS Punjabi

For Satpal Singh, a member of one of the pioneering Sikh families in Woolgoolga, the growth of these celebrations is also a reflection of how the community has held on to its cultural roots across generations.

"Woolgoolga is a bit time-locked in that sense that the Punjab our ancestors brought with them, we still carry it forward," he tells SBS Punjabi.

He has witnessed Diwali evolve from a festival barely acknowledged in the region to now being introduced to children at local schools.

Yet for him, preserving one's heritage has never meant being any less Australian.

I don't think my life would be complete without things that Australia has given me. But I'm still deep-rooted in my own faith, so I am an Australian Sikh.

title: Australia's biggest cultural project since the Opera House goes live
text:
IN BRIEF NSW Premier Chris Minns and Arts Minister John Graham officially opened the Powerhouse Parramatta on Saturday.

An opening festival running over three weeks and four weekends will feature 179 events, most of which are free.

After almost 15 years, the doors of Australia's newest museum, Powerhouse Parramatta, are officially open to the public.

The billion-dollar museum has been described as the largest cultural infrastructure project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House.

About 3,000 objects are on display across 18,000 square metres of exhibition and public space, making it the state's largest museum. On its opening weekend, 25,000 visitors have registered to attend events.

The museum's interim CEO, Abbie Galvin, has said it's wonderful to see the project finally completed.

"It is now a building that is for the community of Western Sydney, the community of New South Wales and of course, Australia," she said. "It is an incredible cultural institution."

"And it represents innovation. It represents education. And it absolutely represents wonderment."

NSW Premier Chris Minns and Arts Minister John Graham opened the riverfront building on Saturday, saying it would be a magnet for Australians looking to spend time engaging with science and culture for free.

Some of the museum's exhibitions do, however, have an entry fee.

Powerhouse Parramatta's opening festival program will run until 29 November. Credit: Powerhouse Studios

Minns also credited former Coalition premier Mike Baird for beginning the project, telling reporters that his party had been wrongly critical of it when in opposition.

"We were wrong," Minns said. "This is fantastic. This is going to be great for Western Sydney. It’s going to be great for NSW," he said.

The opposition, too, was keen to highlight its contribution.

"Western Sydney has been waiting for its fair share and the Liberals and Nationals have delivered. If Labor had won the election in either 2015 or 2019, Powerhouse Parramatta would not be here today," it said in a joint statement.

Powerhouse Parramatta to become global destination

The striking building is covered in a lattice made of 1,300 individual pieces of steel and is the first public building in Australia awarded six green stars under the Green Building Council of Australia's new rating system.

It has a 24-hour accessible outdoor space with gardens, amphitheatres, and promenades linking the Parramatta River to Phillip Street.

An opening festival program over three weeks and four weekends will feature 179 different events, the majority of which are free, across First Nations' culture, science and technology, design, music, film and food.

Acclaimed British artist Es Devlin, whose works make up part of the opening exhibitions, has said she thinks the new museum will become a global destination.

Es Devlin's The Turning installation is one of Powerhouse Parramatta's opening exhibitions. Credit: Powerhouse Studios

"It's the first time that the building gets to sing," she told ABC Radio about the opening. "It's almost like the builders have been crafting this Stradivarius [violin] for seven years, and now is the first time it's given its voice and it meets its public."

"This one is really in a class of its own."

The Sydney Morning Herald has reported that the opening day of the Powerhouse Parramatta is "packed", with crowds and queues for each of the five opening exhibitions.

Attendees have described the building as "instantly iconic" and said that, despite the long wait and the political battles over it, the new Powerhouse appears to have been worth it.

Powerhouse Parramatta's predecessor, Powerhouse Ultimo, is undergoing a $300 million heritage restoration and rebuild project on its 1988 structure. While it too has been delayed by controversies and budget blowouts, it is anticipated to open in late 2028 or early 2029.

title: The grim news for Australian travellers quietly updated this week
text:
In brief Qantas said this week that it would continue to adjust fares and capacity in response to higher fuel costs.

Meanwhile, Westpac has said a surprising number of Australians are ahead on their mortgage repayments.

Australians could soon face higher airfares and fewer flights as Qantas responds to rising fuel costs. Meanwhile, shoppers hoping for big bargains as David Jones enters voluntary administration could be left disappointed.

And as interest rates rise again, new figures reveal just how far ahead some borrowers are on their repayments.

Qantas airfares to rise

Australians love to travel, but they'll soon have to pay even more for the privilege.

In a market update issued this week, Qantas said it would continue to adjust fares and capacity in response to higher fuel costs.

That means more expensive tickets for consumers, and fewer flights to choose from on certain routes. The cuts will be coming from its domestic operations.

However, it would appear that more recent price increases haven't deterred Qantas' customers, with the company saying demand remains resilient.

The carrier said international demand across its Qantas and Jetstar brands remains strong, with flyers redirecting travel away from the Middle East.

Of course, those international jaunts may give travellers something to think about, depending on their destination.

The Australian dollar lost around 2 per cent over the week, roughing up the exchange rate for certain popular holiday spots.

David Jones bargains uncertain

It's quite common for retailers entering voluntary administration to hold major sales and offload some excess inventory, but it might be a little different for David Jones — there could be less to sell.

This week, the iconic Australian department store called in a team to manage the business after it wound up in financial trouble.

However, as University of Technology retail expert Gary Mortimer told SBS' On the Money Podcast, David Jones operates a largely concession-based model under which brands retain control.

"They own that space, they own that inventory, they own that staff," Mortimer said.

READ MORE How David Jones could emerge from administration a very different retailer

"It's likely those brands will go in and collect that inventory whilst they can and move it to their physical store assets."

The administrators are now working through restructuring options, including the closure of some stores. That's where some bargains may ultimately be found.

"If it's a David Jones' branded product, you'd expect to see either some discounting or ideally maybe moving that inventory to stores that will be retained," Mortimer said.

David Jones is the world's oldest continuously running department store still operating under the same name.

Are you ahead on your repayments?

While the Reserve Bank's fifth interest-rate hike of the year will be painful for many, it would appear there are some borrowers who may be able to absorb that increase.

This week, Westpac revealed 37 per cent of its customers are more than two years ahead on their repayments.

In fact, 53 per cent have buffers of six months at the very least. Just 1 per cent of customers are behind.

Nevertheless, this week's RBA rate rise will likely add $107 per month to the repayments of a typical $700,000 loan over 25 years.

The big four banks will pass on their new rates on Black Friday — which, perhaps somewhat ironically, is also Friday the 13th.

title: Chris v Chris: What to know about New Zealand's tightly wedged election
text:
In Brief Chris Luxon and Chris Hipkins are locked in a tight race to lead New Zealand's next government.

Minor parties could hold the balance of power in an election expected to be too close to call.

Across the Tasman, New Zealanders are preparing to head to the polls in what is shaping up to be a tightly contested election.

It will be a battle of two Chrises.

In one corner is Christopher Luxon, the current prime minister and leader of the centre-right National Party, who is seeking a second term leading his coalition government.

In the other is Chris Hipkins, the leader of the centre-left Labour Party, who briefly served as prime minister after Jacinda Ardern resigned in 2023 before losing office later that year.

With campaigning now wrapped up, New Zealanders will vote on Saturday 7 November to decide who forms the country's next government.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Here's what you need to know.

Who are the two main players?

Chris Luxon, National Party

Luxon is New Zealand's current prime minister and has led the country since 2023.

The former Air New Zealand chief executive led the centre-right National Party back into government after defeating Labour three years ago.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is hoping for a second term under his conservative coalition. Source: AAP / Ben Mckay

His campaign has focused heavily on the economy, including plans to return the budget to surplus and expand New Zealand's KiwiSaver retirement scheme.

But his first term has been turbulent. Luxon survived two confidence votes from National MPs this year amid weak polling, economic pressure and tensions within his governing coalition.

Chris Hipkins, Labour

Hipkins is seeking to return Labour to government three years after its election defeat.

The 48-year-old became prime minister in January 2023 following Jacinda Ardern's resignation, but served for less than a year before losing office at the October election.

Since then, he has campaigned on cost of living relief, stronger public services and investment in housing, infrastructure and healthcare.

Former New Zealand prime minister Chris Hipkins is hoping to get back into the top job after losing power in 2023. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

How do New Zealand elections work?

New Zealand uses what's known as a mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system.

Voters cast two votes: one for their local electorate representative and one for the political party they want to govern.

People of Māori descent can choose whether to enrol on the general electoral roll or the Māori electoral roll.

Parliament is usually made up of 120 seats. Seventy-one are elected from geographic electorates, including seven Māori electorates, while the remainder are allocated according to each party's share of the nationwide vote.

A party generally needs at least 5 per cent of the party vote, or to win an electorate seat, to enter parliament.

Because seats are allocated proportionally, it is uncommon for a single party to win an outright majority.

That means coalition governments are the norm.

Every government since MMP was introduced in 1996 has relied on support from smaller parties, with the exception of Jacinda Ardern's Labour government in 2020.

Why the minor parties could decide the result

While much of the attention has focused on Luxon and Hipkins, smaller parties could ultimately determine who forms the next government.

Polling suggests neither National nor Labour is likely to win enough seats to govern alone, making coalition negotiations crucial.

These are the parties likely to play a major role:

New Zealand First: Led by veteran politician Winston Peters, the right-wing populist party is campaigning on issues including immigration, energy prices and withdrawing from the Paris climate agreement.

ACT : Led by deputy prime minister David Seymour, the libertarian-leaning party has focused on immigration, crime and reducing the size of government.

The Greens: Labour's most likely coalition partner, campaigning on climate action, tax reform and cost-of-living measures, including a proposed wealth tax.

Te Pāti Māori: Focused on Māori rights and representation, and expected to retain several Māori electorates.

Opportunity (TOP) : A centrist party led by Qiulae Wong that has never won a seat in parliament but is hovering around the 5 per cent threshold needed to enter parliament and could become a kingmaker.

What are the main issues for voters?

Like many countries around the world, the cost of living remains New Zealand's top election issue.

Inflation has eased from earlier highs, but households continue to face pressure from petrol prices, housing costs and everyday expenses.

The country's unemployment rate has risen to 5.7 per cent, its highest level in 11 years, while economic growth has remained sluggish following a prolonged downturn.

Healthcare has also emerged as a major campaign issue amid concerns about strained hospitals, staffing shortages and long waiting times for treatment.

Housing affordability remains a longstanding problem, particularly for younger New Zealanders trying to enter the property market.

Immigration, government spending, climate policy and Māori issues have also featured prominently throughout the campaign.

What's at stake on Indigenous issues?

The election comes after years of heated debate about Māori rights and representation, particularly around the Treaty of Waitangi, New Zealand's founding agreement between Māori leaders and the British Crown.

The coalition government has rolled back several policies designed to give Māori greater representation in public decision-making, while ACT has campaigned against what it calls "race-based" policies and has proposed abolishing the Waitangi Tribunal.

Meanwhile, Te Pāti Māori has sought to mobilise Indigenous voters and frame the election as a pivotal moment for Māori representation.

Because the overall contest is so close, the outcome in the seven Māori electorates could also influence coalition negotiations after election day.

What does the polling indicate?

Most polls suggest the race is too close to call.

The latest poll from Post-Freshwater Strategy, released on Friday, placed the opposition Labour Party slightly ahead, but still with no clear outcome for the election.

But it also placed the Opportunity Party at 5.1 per cent — just above the threshold for representation in parliament. If it crosses that line, it could emerge as a kingmaker in coalition talks.

Another October poll from Roy Morgan placed the centre-right bloc of National, ACT and NZ First as holding a narrow lead over Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori.

Another poll by Infrastructure New Zealand, an industry association, released on Friday, put Labour at 30.7 per cent and National at 26.4 per cent.

Analysts have also noted growing support for smaller parties, reflecting frustration among some voters with New Zealand's two major parties.

When is New Zealand's election and when will we know the results?

New Zealanders will head to the polls on Saturday 7 November, with voting closing at 7pm local time (5pm AEDT).

More than 1.4 million votes had already been cast during advance voting by the middle of election week.

Early results are expected to start emerging shortly after polls close, but New Zealand may not know who will form government on election night.

If no party wins enough seats to govern outright, major parties will need to negotiate coalition or support agreements with smaller parties, a process that can take days or even weeks.

That places the centrist Opportunity Party in a unique position. The party says it is willing to work with either side of politics and, if it enters parliament, could have significant influence over who forms New Zealand's next government.

What is clear, however, is that whichever major party wins the most votes is likely to need support from at least one smaller party, meaning coalition negotiations could ultimately decide who becomes New Zealand's next prime minister.

— With additional reporting by Australian Associated Press and Reuters.

title: How the US midterm results could 'cascade through' the AI and data centre industry
text:
In Brief Democratic candidates have been elected in several key states currently at the centre of data centre growth.

The results of this week's midterm elections have prompted significant drops in tech stocks internationally.

This week, voters in 13 US states were asked more than just who they wanted to represent them in Congress — they were also asked about a controversial new fixture in their neighbourhood: data centres.

According to analysis by Ballotpedia, at least 50 local ballot measures related to data centres.

The non-profit, which provides ballot information to voters around the country, tracked propositions put to voters across Arkansas, California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio and Wisconsin.

With three measures left to be decided later in the year, voters in the United States overwhelmingly rejected the development of data centres in their area.

All but one of the ballot measures failed.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The exception was in the small town of Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected an additional review of industrial projects, including data centres.

The largest proportion of motions were put to voters in Ohio, with 21 measures rejected across 18 jurisdictions.

It's one of several key states for data centre development, including Virginia, Texas, Georgia, California and Illinois.

Thousands of data centres have already been built across the US. Source: SBS News

Texas Democrat governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned to increase regulation and promised a moratorium on data centre construction. She is one of many pro-regulation candidates elected.

The trend has started to concern analysts, as shares in AI companies and tech-heavy stock indexes fell sharply on Thursday.

The US has far more data centres than any other country in the world following explosive growth in the past year.

The market reaction

The midterm results came as US stock markets had their worst day in 19 months amid fears of an AI slowdown as sellers shift stock that now carries risk.

Chipmaker Nvidia's shares dropped by at least 9 per cent, reducing its market value by US$400 billion ($580 billion). Shares in AMD and Micron, which also produce parts needed for AI computing, dropped more than 17 per cent.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq finished at least 5.5 per cent lower, according to Dow Jones data, while Japan's Nikkei 225 also fell as Asian chipmakers suffered.

Brad Conger, chief investment officer at investment firm Hirtle & Co, said the sell-off was the result of several factors, including concerns about ongoing financing and regulation of data centres.

"Some investors have reached the limit where they just have to liquidate risk entirely," he told Reuters.

Australia's markets largely avoided the global rout, with the ASX much more bank than tech-focused.

Chief investment officer at Opal Capital Management, Omkar Joshi, told SBS News' On the Money podcast the major falls in the US, Japan and South Korean exchanges are likely a symptom of reality setting in after overspend on AI, but he said it's not necessarily a case of the bubble popping.

"Funding costs have been blowing out for a while now, and it's really more just a reset of that reality rather than anything else that's coming through now.

"There was a lot of investor optimism in (the AI) space, and there wasn't always a lot of rationality on certain elements of the market."

He said the market reaction has created a "difficult" environment for Anthropic, which is preparing to launch the world's biggest public offering.

Trump has blamed the crash on the Democrats, only a day after celebrating what he called "another record high" for the stock market.

"The stock market suffered one of the worst days in history based on the results of the election," he said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

"Such a sad thing to watch! It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this."

For some investors, it's been a clear sign of public sentiment.

"In our view, the significance of these midterm elections is more like a referendum on AI than a referendum on (Donald) Trump," Aidan Yao, a senior investment strategist at the Amundi Investment Institute, told Reuters.

What happens now?

Tapas Strickland, CEO of share trading platform Moomoo Australia, warned the governor's races in Texas and Georgia could significantly slow infrastructure rollout.

"Those two states effectively make up about a third of all AI data centre spend and projects," he told Reuters.

"If both of those go Democrat at the governor level, the potential for it to slow is very much there, and that would obviously cascade through to the rest of the AI sector."

Hinojosa and fellow Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms both won their seats with considerable margins. Bottoms and Amy Acton, governor-elect of Ohio, have also supported moratoriums on large data centre construction.

A slowdown in data-centre infrastructure could further impact not only the financial stability of operators, but also energy producers, chipmakers and cloud companies.

The impact could extend beyond the US, as operators look to more advantageous jurisdictions.

One potential result, according to analysts at HSBC, is that data centre operators move to more lenient states or countries should incoming leaders increase regulation.

title: More than three months after the World Cup, why haven't the Socceroos been paid?
text:
in brief Some Socceroos are still chasing Football Australia for 2026 FIFA World Cup pay.

The team has also petitioned have their match in Jordan moved due to the war in the Middle East.

Socceroos players who competed at this year's FIFA World Cup in North America are yet to be paid their match fees, three months after the tournament finished.

Just days after it was revealed that both male and female national team players were taking legal action against Football Australia (FA) over their revenue-sharing agreement, members of the 2026 Socceroos World Cup squad are pursuing Australia's football governing body for match payments.

Payment was due within a fortnight of the date they broke camp.

Australia were knocked out of the tournament at the round-of-32 stage in a loss to Egypt on 3 July.

FA, which recorded a $23 million loss over the last two financial years, said tax complications in the United States caused the delay.

The body said it was working with the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia (PFA), to "resolve the outstanding matters as quickly as possible" and that it was ready to make the payments.

"Before those payments can be processed, however, we require final specialist advice on the North American taxation obligations applicable to the payments, as well as some further player distribution information being provided through the PFA," FA said in a statement.

"Recognising the complexity of North American taxation requirements, FIFA facilitated access to specialist tax support for all participating member associations to help them understand and meet their respective obligations.

"We have been actively engaging with those specialist advisers since the World Cup to confirm the applicable tax and withholding treatment."

If a player sees game time, or is an unused substitute for the national team, they earn around $6,000 in match fees.

The Socceroos played two friendlies against Mexico and Switzerland before three World Cup group games and the Egypt shootout defeat, meaning players named for all six games are heading into camp this week out of pocket by roughly $36,000.

There were no known payment issues for the four friendlies which took place in the US in the October and November windows last year.

READ MORE Socceroos' next test to go ahead despite Saudi Arabia airport attacks

PFA chief executive Beau Busch said the situation was unacceptable.

"Any matter related to international tax was foreseeable and should have been addressed long before a ball was kicked at the tournament," he said.

Members of the squad who faced Brazil in two friendlies in Queensland in September are understood to have been paid in full.

Socceroos petition for Jordan match to move

FA's delay in paying World Cup match fees comes as players head into November's friendly window in the Middle East.

Some players have expressed concerns about travelling to the region — Australia will face Qatar in Doha and Jordan in Amman — amid the wider conflict.

The purpose of those friendlies in the current climate has been brought into question since the Asian Football Confederation opted to delay the Asian Cup.

Socceroos players, via their union, have urged FA to reschedule or relocate their upcoming friendly against Jordan in Amman due to safety concerns.

The Asian Football Confederation postponed that tournament, originally scheduled for January-February in Saudi Arabia, following the attack on Riyadh's international airport by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

The Socceroos squad was expected to be named on Friday, but the announcement has been pushed back to the weekend amid uncertainty over whether some players will withdraw.

Indonesia's football association has already cancelled a 13 November planned friendly against Jordan in Amman amid an escalation in violence in the area, and the PFA made it clear Australian players didn't want to proceed.

"The PFA has worked with Football Australia over recent weeks in relation to security concerns regarding the upcoming assembly and engaged its own independent security experts," Busch said.

"With the full support of the PFA, the players have overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated.

"We are committed to working with FA to reach a sensible solution."

title: These Kiwis were driven to Australia by rising costs. Could an election bring them home?
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Despite working fewer hours and earning less, the Ririnui family has more money left over each week on the Gold Coast than they did in Auckland.

Tajai Ririnui, 32, her husband, and three daughters moved from New Zealand just three months ago after struggling to make ends meet amid a cost of living crisis that showed little sign of easing.

"After rent, fuel, kindy, groceries and putting money aside for things like power, water and internet, we were left with next to nothing," she tells SBS News.

"Don't get me wrong, we had everything we needed, but there was no room to save, no room for extra activities with our girls and very little opportunity to actually enjoy life.”

Ririnui's husband Jayden, 31, worked in floor restoration in New Zealand, putting in 12-hour days, sometimes six or seven days a week, to support the family. He now works as a scaffolder on the Gold Coast.

"We're averaging below what we were getting in New Zealand, but we have more left over, which is ironic because we're working less," Tajai says.

The pull home is very strong, but honestly, you'd rather … have everything and that little bit more here than be broke and have nothing at home.

Tajai Ririnui and her family moved to the Gold Coast due to the high cost of living in New Zealand. Source: Supplied

The Ririnuis are not alone.

Australia's higher wages and broader employment opportunities have long drawn New Zealanders across the Tasman, where they can live and work indefinitely under the Trans-Tasman Travel Arrangement. The movement has continued even as the economic gap between the two countries has fluctuated over time.

In the year to March 2026, an estimated 47,900 New Zealanders moved to Australia, while about 19,900 New Zealanders moved in the opposite direction, leaving a net migration loss of about 27,900 people, according to Stats NZ.

But beyond the headline migration figures, new research suggests more young New Zealanders are leaving for Australia and elsewhere overseas for the long term, raising concerns about the country's economic future.

As New Zealanders prepare to vote in Saturday's general election, the question is whether the next government can turn the tide and convince more of them to stay.

Why Kiwis are leaving

Former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern renewed attention on the country's emigration debate when she settled on Sydney's Northern Beaches earlier this year.

She joined the nearly 620,000 New Zealand-born people already living in Australia as of 2024 — representing about one in eight Kiwis.

Source: SBS News

The number of arrivals ebbs and flows depending on how each country's economy is performing. But a new report suggests more young people are making the move with little intention of returning.

About 77,500 New Zealanders aged 18 to 30 left the country long term for Australia and elsewhere between 2023 and 2025 — 60 per cent above the pre-pandemic average — according to Victor Consulting research commissioned by New Zealand's Green Party.

Of those who left, more than four in 10 are not expected to return, according to the research, potentially resulting in the permanent loss of NZ$12 billion ($9.7 billion) in education and healthcare investment.

Paul Spoonley, a New Zealand sociologist and emeritus professor at Massey University, says young New Zealanders have traditionally left in two groups: school leavers and graduates in their mid-20s.

He links the recent departures to graduates struggling to find work in New Zealand while Australian employers actively recruit, particularly in health and policing.

The Auckland skyline. The number of arrivals from New Zealand to Australia often depends on how each economy is performing. Source: Bloomberg / Becki Moss

Historically, around half of New Zealanders who moved to Australia eventually returned to New Zealand, but Spoonley suspects a larger share of the current wave may stay overseas.

"What we'd normally expect is that as the economic conditions in New Zealand improve over the medium to short, long term, then the migration would ease," he tells SBS News.

But I'm not sure that those economic conditions in New Zealand are going to be as short-term as we thought.

New Zealand has experienced a years-long economic downturn, with two recessions since 2022. Although the economy has begun to recover, unemployment remains elevated at 5.7 per cent, an 11-year high, compared with 4.7 per cent in Australia.

Last month, New Zealand finance minister Nicola Willis announced the National Party's election commitments to encourage young Kiwis to stay or return home. These include plans to legislate for lower student loan repayments, expand a 5 per cent home deposit scheme and extend paid parental leave, if the coalition government is returned to office.

But New Zealand economist Shamubeel Eaqub is sceptical there is an easy solution to stemming the flow of people overseas, pointing to four decades of faster wage growth in Australia.

Economist Shamubeel Eaqub says there are no easy solutions to entice New Zealanders to stay. Source: Supplied

In 2009, then prime minister John Key set a target of closing the income gap with Australia by 2025 — a goal that was never met.

"Obviously, we didn't, and so therein lies the issue. Politicians have learned from that a little bit, and they're less gung-ho about proclaiming they're going to somehow close the gap with Australia," Eaqub tells SBS News.

The cost of staying

Another New Zealander planning to make the move is Lisa Robb, 47, who has lived in Katikati, a town of 6,000 people roughly two hours' drive south-east of Auckland, with her family for 23 years.

After work dried up for her husband Manny's plastering business, he moved to Perth in February.

Lisa Robb (third from the left) is planning to join her husband, Manny (third from the right), in Perth after her youngest son finishes school. Source: Supplied

In New Zealand, he often worked seven days a week. In Perth, he now earns three times as much while working Monday to Friday, Robb says.

Two of her adult children have already moved to Australia in search of better opportunities, as have her stepson and his young family.

She plans to join them after her 15-year-old son finishes school.

"You just don't get to live a life because you're too busy working to make the money that you need just to survive, not even thrive, just survive," Robb tells SBS News.

"We wouldn't even have considered it if we didn't need to."

I love my country … I love the culture here, I love my trees and my birds, and all the rest of it, but if you can't afford to live then you can't afford to live.

While some inflationary pressures, including global energy and commodity price shocks, are beyond the government's control, Robb believes domestic policy could do more to ease the pressure on households.

"If they want people to stop leaving New Zealand, then they have to make New Zealand a more attractive place to live and at the moment, New Zealand isn't an attractive place to live," she says.

"I don't know what the answer is ... I just know that I live here, and I have to pay my bills, and I can't afford to do that because of how expensive things are."

While economic factors remain the biggest driver of emigration, Mark Berger, who runs relocation company NZ Relo, says families are often chasing something harder to measure.

Source: SBS News

"It's all about hope … it's someone thinking about their future and how they can apply it to better their family and their circumstances," he tells SBS News.

A knife-edge contest

Saturday's election is shaping up as a tight contest, with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National Party polling at 30 per cent and the opposition Labour Party, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins, on 29 per cent, according to the latest 1News Verian poll.

Government coalition parties ACT New Zealand and New Zealand First polled 10 per cent and 8 per cent respectively, leaving the right-wing bloc with a projected 58 seats — three short of the 61 needed for a majority in New Zealand's 120-seat parliament.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon (centre) has promised to cut government spending if re-elected. Source: Getty / Hagen Hopkins

The left-wing bloc, comprising Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori (the Māori Party), would secure 56 or 60 seats, depending on the outcome of the Māori electorate contests and potential parliamentary overhangs.

The poll also puts the Opportunity Party on 6 per cent, potentially giving it seven MPs and a significant say in post-election coalition negotiations. Neither major bloc is projected to secure a majority on its own.

The election is being fought against a backdrop of mounting pressure on household budgets.

An Ipsos poll released last week found 64 per cent of respondents believed the cost of living was the country's biggest issue, followed by healthcare at 45 per cent, fuel prices (31 per cent), the economy (30 per cent) and unemployment (19 per cent).

While inflation has eased from its post-pandemic peak, it remained at 3.7 per cent in the 12 months to September, above the Reserve Bank's target range of 1 to 3 per cent. Although down from 4.1 per cent in the year to June, many households have yet to experience sustained relief.

National's approach to tackling the cost of living centres on cutting government spending — including reducing the public service workforce by nearly 9,000 – and delivering tax relief.

Labour, meanwhile, has pledged to reduce household bills through free GP visits, capped public transport fares, a freeze on fuel taxes, and greater supermarket regulation. Its proposed capital gains tax on investment and commercial property would help fund its healthcare commitments.

Opposition leader Chris Hipkins' Labour Party is polling neck-and-neck with the National-led government. Source: Bloomberg / Brendon O'Hagan

Although frustrated with the pace of progress under National, Robb says she is leaning towards voting for either National or ACT New Zealand.

To be quite honest, I'd like a change, but that's really not going to make much difference.

"I like the way National is going; I just wish they'd get there a little bit faster. I think a lot of the problems that we have are COVID hang-ups, which really you can't blame on the government 100 per cent."

Tajai Ririnui, meanwhile, is hoping Labour will take office, believing a change of government could bring relief to middle-and lower-income families.

As a Māori woman, she sees the current National-led government's policy changes affecting Māori as another setback. She would like to see Te Pāti Māori in government but considers that unlikely.

"Our government seems determined to undermine Māori culture, and honestly, the state of things back home is heartbreaking," she says.

We are a minority, unfortunately, in New Zealand … we get treated as kind of like outsiders in our own country.

Since taking power in 2023, the National-led government has abolished the independent Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora), prioritised English in official communications and backed the Treaty Principles Bill, which sought to redefine aspects of how the Treaty of Waitangi is interpreted. The bill was defeated at its second reading in April 2025.

Thousands protested in 2024 when the junior coalition party ACT New Zealand proposed legislation to redefine the founding treaty between Māori and the Crown. Source: Bloomberg / Mark Coote

The government has defended its approach as promoting equal treatment and common understanding of public services and the law.

New Zealand's Electoral Commission says about 126,000 enrolled voters have told it they are living overseas — up from 92,600 in 2023 — with the majority in Australia.

Spoonley says the growing number of overseas voters could be significant, given the traditionally younger demographic of New Zealanders living abroad and their potential influence on the election result.

"We've got people who've left New Zealand in the last two years ... who I suspect are quite disgruntled with some of the policy settings, and want to know that they're going to get a government that is more sympathetic.”

Would they ever return?

While Robb is a proud New Zealander, she struggles to see herself returning to New Zealand anytime soon once she's established a life in Australia.

"Everybody I know that's left New Zealand is loyal to New Zealand and wouldn't have left if they didn't have to," she says.

Lisa Robb says doesn't expect to return to New Zealand until she retires. Source: Supplied

"I will work out the rest of my working years in Australia," Robb says.

I don't want to die [in Australia], but New Zealand has to drastically change before I would consider coming back here, and I don't see that happening before I retire.

Ririnui, however, says the plan is to return home

"We moved to Australia for the money, and that's it. Our goal is to put our heads down, work hard and save as much as we possibly can over the next five, 10 years, with the hope of eventually returning home.

"Being Māori, we're spiritually and wholeheartedly connected to our whenua [land] and our whānau [extended family]. And even though we've only been away for a short time, we can feel that something is missing from our lives. Even our girls feel it."

title: Why doctors are writing medical scripts for fresh air
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive NationalHealthcare Why doctors are writing medical scripts for fresh air Henrietta Cook November 8, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
