When three-time cancer survivor Sarina Sorrenti and her husband, Sam Pitruzzello, visit their GP, they don’t just leave with scripts for pharmaceutical medications – their doctor also prescribes nature. “Nature walking,” GP Vicki Kotsirilos wrote on a recent script for Sorrenti, alongside a list of vitamins. Sarina Sorrenti and Sam Pitruzzello are among a growing number of Australians benefiting from “nature dosing”. Justin McManus The pair follow the doctor’s orders faithfully, regularly walking beneath the towering gums that line the banks of a billabong near their home in Melbourne’s north. “It’s about absorbing and noticing all the details, everything from the bark on the tree trunk, to the branches, even the leaves,” says Pitruzzello, who has a rare medical condition called myositis, which leads to muscle weakness and pain. “It’s not just ‘go for a walk for exercise’ – now it’s time to heal.”

Advertisement

For the first time, the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) has endorsed new guidelines for prescribing nature. Related Article Science A nature prescription could be just what the doctor ordered Developed by the not-for-profit People and Parks Foundation, the Nature Dose resource details how GPs can prescribe the outdoors for patients as part of their routine care. More intentional than simply being in nature, the practice requires people to make a point of tuning in to sights, sounds, smells and textures. This might include walking near water, feeling the texture of bark or listening to the sound of insects and birds. The guidelines state as little as 20 minutes a day, or two hours a week, can reduce stress, improve mood and wellbeing, enhance sleep and reduce blood pressure. Nature dosing is offered to patients in addition to traditional medical treatment, and is always individualised. People and Parks director Alison Hill says “intergenerational indoorsness” has led to a situation where many people no longer experience the benefits of nature.

Advertisement

She believes this disconnect from nature is fuelling existential crises like climate change, and leading to poor mental health and chronic diseases. “Part of the solution is helping people reconnect with nature and remember that they are part of [it],” she says. “This helps them realise that when we are caring for nature, we are also caring for ourselves now and into the future.” People and Parks director Alison Hill While a growing body of evidence supports the movement, many of the sample sizes are small and rely on self-reporting. A recent UK study of 171 participants found nature prescribing significantly improved wellbeing while reducing symptoms of anxiety and depression.

Advertisement

In Australia, a study of 39 young people with mild to moderate mental health issues found two hours of weekly nature dosing improved their wellbeing, easing psychological distress and significantly reducing loneliness. The participants, who lived in the Shepparton area in northern Victoria, went on bushwalks and engaged in nature journaling, yoga, tree planting and nature photography. A larger UK study of almost 20,000 participants found spending at least two hours a week in nature was linked to significantly greater self-reported health and wellbeing. Advocates have several theories about why nature dosing works. It could provide an escape from the stresses of modern living, or diversify the body’s microbiome through exposure to different bacteria and fungi. Or perhaps, our bodies are simply designed to thrive in the natural world.

Advertisement

Dr Kuljit Singh, the national chair of the RACGP’s social prescribing specific interests group, says while anyone can spend time in nature, a formal nudge, as well as guidance from a doctor, can make all the difference. “It’s empowering,” the Gold Coast-based GP says. “The doctor is telling you to do this, and you are doing it to prevent illness. It gives patients an alternative to a prescription, or a powerful adjunct to one.” Dr Kuljit Singh, the national chair of the RACGP’s social prescribing specific interests group. Singh, who has been prescribing nature to her patients for about 20 years, says the practice is transformative. “It makes a huge difference, from children right through to our seniors,” she says. “For children who have erratic behaviour, panic attacks, or anxiety, spending time looking, listening, and feeling nature really calms them.”

Advertisement

While more than 1000 GPs already prescribe nature to their patients, Singh says the RACGP’s endorsement of the new guidelines will encourage more to follow suit. “When we qualify as doctors, we are always taught to look at lifestyle measures first before we reach for a pill,” she says. “It hasn’t always been given enough weight.” Nature dosing has already been used as part of trials for cancer patients at Alfred Health’s Paula Fox Melanoma and Cancer Centre and at headspace in Shepparton. As part of another study, new parents in the City of Banyule in Melbourne’s north-east were prescribed group-based nature dosing to reduce their risk of loneliness. Vicki Kotsirilos says prescribing nature is a no-brainer. “There is surprisingly lots of evidence demonstrating regular exposure to nature is beneficial to human health physically, mentally, emotionally and spiritually,” she says.

Advertisement

“Nature contact can improve sleep and mental health, reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety, ADHD, reduce aggression, and brings greater happiness, wellbeing, life satisfaction and social connectedness.” The shift has been profound for Sorrenti and Pitruzzello. Pitruzzello and Sorrenti say nature dosing has transformed their health and wellbeing. Justin McManus As frogs croak in the billabong and dragonflies skim the water’s murky surface, Sorrenti says her nervous system is now back in balance. She feels more energised than she did in her 20s and 30s. Her mental health, which took a battering following three separate cancer diagnoses, has also improved. As well as daily walks in nature, Sorrenti stands barefoot in her garden for 15 minutes every morning.

Advertisement

“People just want to go to doctors and ask them to fix them,” she says. “You have to be part of the healing.” For Pitruzzello, regular nature dosing has improved his motivation to stay fit and healthy. It’s also helped him come to terms with having a chronic health condition. “When you have chronic conditions like mine, it affects your mental health,” he says. “You can just get into this spiral ... you want to make sure that you live with it the best you can.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Coastal residents fuming after being hit with $541,000 light bill
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaRoads Coastal residents fuming after being hit with $541,000 light bill Benjamin Preiss November 8, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The residents of Martha Cove are used to paying a premium for their picturesque marina lifestyle. The development in Safety Beach on the Mornington Peninsula is home to about 3000 people who live in properties ranging from apartments to luxury villas. Collectively, they fund the maintenance of boardwalks, underpass lifts, harbour dredging and other features of the area even though the public has right of access. The Martha Cove residential development offers a waterfront lifestyle, but residents pay for the upkeep. Joe Armao But now residents are in a dispute with the Victorian Department of Transport and Planning over its plans to charge them a combined $541,000 to update lights in a public underpass used by motorists daily. Martha Cove Owners Corporation chairman Neil Pope, a former Victorian Labor government minister, said a dated agreement between the developer of Martha Cove, Mornington Peninsula Shire and the department had resulted in residents being saddled with the cost of maintaining public infrastructure.

Advertisement

“This is ultimately an issue of fairness, accountability and the proper use of property owners’ money,” he said. Construction began on the Martha Cove development in 2004, and it was built progressively over the following years. The area now has more than 1800 dwellings and about 830 marina berths for boats. Neil Pope driving in the underpass where the lights will be upgraded. Joe Armao Pope said residents understood they faced additional costs to live in the area, with its associated waterfront access. Last year, residents spent a combined $450,000 on underpass lifts, which are open to the public, as well as replacing a 2.3-kilometre timber boardwalk with fibreglass resin polymer after it became slippery and dangerous. But Pope said it was outrageous the Department of Transport and Planning wanted residents to fund the upgrade of 50 lights in an 80-metre stretch of underpass. The department wants to upgrade the current sodium vapour and fluorescent lights with LED.

Advertisement

“We accept that we have to look after the marina,” Pope said. “But it just makes it darn hard when we have to budget for stuff we don’t believe we should have to pay the full amount for.” Pope served as the state MP for Monbulk from 1982 to 1992. Under the Cain and Kirner governments, he served as the minister for labour, minister for school education and minister for youth affairs. Now he is frustrated with the bureaucracy on his side of politics, and said the department had failed to adequately explain how it reached the figure of $541,000, and hadn’t provided residents with design documents. He also expressed concern about the potentially enormous future costs of maintaining the underpass. “This [cost] is an extraordinary development and one that has caused considerable concern among residents,” he said.

Advertisement

Under a section 173 agreement, which sets out long-term obligations for property owners, residents at Martha Cove are required to fund maintenance and replacements in the area. The light replacement project is due to begin this month. Residents are required to contribute to a sinking fund, which covers infrastructure and maintenance in the marina. With the department able to access that fund, Pope said residents could not stop the department from extracting the money. A bus emerging from the underpass where the lights will be upgraded. Joe Armao Pope said the Martha Cove waterway had fundamentally changed the area, by creating a boating activity destination with access to Port Phillip Bay. A spokesperson for the Department of Transport and Planning said it was working closely with the Martha Cove Owners Corporation to ensure the underpass was maintained in accordance with safety standards.

Advertisement

“As a privately funded development, the owners corporation is responsible for the ongoing operation and maintenance of the Martha Cove underpass,” the spokesperson said. The department said the underpass was built in 2005 to facilitate the lowering of Marina Drive beneath the entrance channel to Martha Cove Marina. Pope says it’s unfair for residents to pay for new lighting in the underpass. Joe Armao The department said the light replacement program addressed performance and reliability issues and complied with the department’s procurement policy. The department also said it had providing briefings and shared information with residents since the project development phase began two years ago. But Liberal MP Anthony Marsh, whose seat of Nepean covers the marina, lashed the department’s handling of the project.

Advertisement

Related Article Summer in Victoria Why the beach wars are hotter than ever this summer “That is a significant cost on local households, especially during a cost-of-living crisis,” Marsh said in a speech to Victorian parliament in September. Marsh said the owners corporation supported replacing ageing lights, but did not accept the “extraordinary bill” without proper scrutiny of the project’s scope and costs. “Martha Cove residents should not be left carrying an unreasonable and avoidable financial burden,” he said. title: Victoria Barracks sale abandoned following backlash
text:
Advertisement

Updated PoliticsFederalDefence Victoria Barracks sale abandoned following backlash Eryk Bagshaw and Harriet Alexander Updated November 8, 2026 — 4:22pm ,first published November 8, 2026 — 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Albanese government has bowed to public pressure and abandoned the sale of Victoria Barracks, removing its most high-profile defence asset from its attempt to claw back $3 billion in taxpayer money. The decision, announced on Sunday, means the 186-year-old Victoria Barracks in Paddington will remain in government hands. Loading The government has also reversed course on selling land containing an ancient Angophora red gum forest inside HMAS Penguin on Sydney Harbour, which will now be handed over to the Sydney Harbour Federation Trust. Victoria Barracks, the colonial-era sandstone military headquarters, will not be sold, but it will also no longer be used as an active Australian Defence Force facility. Instead, it will be opened to the public and the space will be commercialised to fund the maintenance of the building. Part of the site may also be developed.

Advertisement

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had lived in Sydney his whole life and Sunday’s announcement was the first time he had stepped foot inside Victoria Barracks. “This is an asset for Sydney that should be opened up for Sydneysiders,” he said. “Most Sydneysiders have not been to this beautiful site.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Deputy Prime Minster Richard Marles at Victoria Barracks on Sunday. George Chan The move now opens the door to further challenges to the government’s plans to sell off more than 60 other sites around the country. The Headland Preservation Group, which has been protesting plans to sell part of HMAS Penguin at Balmoral on Sydney Harbour, said the decision to hand over the forest to the Sydney Harbour Foreshore Trust while retaining the site’s physical structures and beach for the defence force was a great result.

Advertisement

“It’s the outcome we’ve been advocating for, which is terrific,” said Jill L’Estrange, president of the Headland Preservation Group. “The Sydney Harbour Foreshore Trust is next door – it already manages a large part of the forest and this is another segment of it so it’s really appropriate. They won’t be making any money out of it on this basis, but Albanese had always said that this harbour foreshore needed to be protected so he’s staying true to his word.” An aerial view of the HMAS Penguin naval base at Middle Head. Alamy Marles had until September maintained that Victoria Barracks would be sold, describing it as “the oldest wine cellar in Sydney” used by only a section of the military elite. The comments provoked a backlash from supporters of the site and galvanised the Save Victoria Barracks Alliance. An unlikely coalition of veterans’ groups, former prime ministers Paul Keating, John Howard and Tony Abbott, Premier Chris Minns and federal, state and local politicians all spoke out against the sale of the site.

Advertisement

The Daily Telegraph, which first reported the Albanese government’s backflip on Sunday morning, also campaigned heavily against the sale. Albanese said on Sunday afternoon there were limits on what could be done at the site due to the heritage listing, and the decision to keep it in public hands ensured there would be no interference that would downgrade its heritage significance. He did not rule out the possibility that parts of the site may be put out on a 99-year lease. Politicians including Allegra Spender, Alex Greenwich, John Howard and Tony Abbott joined the Victoria Barracks protest. Oscar Colman “What we’re open to is making sure that there’s proper use of the site, it’s respected, and in terms of commercial opportunities that are there, they’ll be explored,” he said. The government announced three other Defence sites, including Victoria Barracks and Point Cook in Melbourne and Fort Queenscliff near Geelong, would remain publicly owned and opened up for community access.

Advertisement

Marles said the government remained committed to moving Defence personnel off the four sites within two years, and the Australian War Memorial would be commissioned to “interpret” the sites and tell their stories. “In respect of the stories which relate to defence, which are captured in these buildings, those stories will be told in a bigger and better way to a much larger audience, which is a much better heritage outcome,” Marles said. “We need to have a defence force that is focused. Every person who wears our nation’s uniform matters. Every hour they spend counts, and every dollar which resources them is precious. Which is why we are making these decisions.” Loading NSW Premier Chris Minns said stopping the sale was the right decision.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Planning The price of Victoria Barracks is much higher than $200 million Nadia Teong Clinical psychologist “I’m glad they’ve made this call, and I congratulate them for it,” he said. “I think [the heritage] would have been lost if it was sold off to a private developer.” The government estimated maintaining the site as a defence facility would cost $200 million over the next 10 years. But stopping the sale of Victoria Barracks will still punch a hole worth hundreds of millions of dollars in the government’s attempt to recoup $3 billion from ailing defence assets. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said he would fight to keep the sites in Defence hands, as well as HMAS Penguin, Lancer Barracks, and Irwin Barracks. NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane expanded the list to include Randwick Barracks.

Advertisement

“This was never about modernising the Defence estate – it was just another smash and grab for revenue by a Prime Minister who can’t manage money and can’t control his spending,” Taylor said in a statement on X. City of Sydney councillor Zann Maxwell, who has campaigned for Victoria Barracks to be part of the solution to housing supply shortages in inner suburbs, said the government’s new position was consistent with everything the community wanted. Related Article Defence Marles wants Defence out of $3 billion sites ‘as soon as possible’ This included public ownership, public access, provision of housing and for the historic buildings to be repurposed for civic, cultural and appropriate commercial activities. “Those who argued the site should remain a closed-off military base for the exclusive use of a small part of the army still won’t be happy, but this is the right call,” Maxwell said.

Advertisement

“The gates are opening. Now we get to decide together what will happen on the other side.” With Michael McGowan Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

title: Young couple pays $4.25m for mid-century modern northern beaches home
text:
Advertisement

PropertyNewsAuctions Young couple pays $4.25m for mid-century modern northern beaches home Elizabeth Redman November 8, 2026 — 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A young couple paid $4.25 million for an eye-catching mid-century modern house in Clontarf, in a hard-fought Saturday auction that defied Sydney’s weak property market. The five-bedroom house at 26 Cutler Road featured timber beams, exposed brick interiors, a fireplace, a cantilevered concrete slab and views over Middle Harbour. The property was one of 964 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 49 per cent from 571 reported results throughout the week, while 222 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. It was the first test of the market’s reaction to the Reserve Bank’s fifth cash rate hike for the year on Tuesday, to 4.85 per cent. Although the clearance rate remains at weak levels, it was a similar result to last week’s early read of 48 per cent, as many buyers already in the market may have factored the rate rise into their budgets.

Advertisement

Eight parties registered for the Clontarf home. Bidding began at $3.55 million, below the price guide of $3.9 million, and rose rapidly at first. Two locals dropped out of the race first, leaving it to two out-of-area buyers to compete until the hammer fell at $4.25 million. title: $2b and plenty of new seats: Inside airlines’ battle for first-class supremacy
text:

BusinessCompaniesAviation $2b and plenty of new seats: Inside airlines’ battle for first-class supremacy Chris Zappone November 8, 2026 — 2:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. With high-paying passengers driving airline profitability, carriers are locked in an escalating race to outshine one another through what they offer in their premium cabins. Singapore Airlines has revealed the seats to be installed in many of its A350s as part of a long-awaited $S2 billion ($2.26 billion) cabin refit – for first class, business class, premium economy and economy. The new cabins will also be in its upcoming order of 31 Boeing 777-9s. The complexity and cost of the cabin refit tells a much broader story about the battle to cater to the premium traveller with better seating, cabins, service and food. That battle is playing out against the constraints of the industry as it struggles to keep up with surging demand for seats. The Singapore Airlines refit was announced in 2024 with expectations the first of 41 A350-900 planes would be ready by this year. Instead, the airline said this year that the first planes would start to be refitted by the first quarter of 2027, the revised timeline reflecting what it said were industry-wide supply chain constraints and a delay in the certification of one of the new seats.

Advertisement

Safety regulators such as the US Federal Aviation Administration certify planes and interiors for flight. Singapore Airlines senior vice president customer experience Yeoh Phee Teik told a press conference on Friday: “Seats have already been certified on the 777-9. As you know, the 777-9 aircraft itself has not yet passed certification.” Loading “You have to understand the intricacies of that; the seats on the A350 have not yet been certified. We are undergoing that process right now.” Which is to say seats for a plane not yet cleared for use are approved, but new seats for a plane already in use (the A350) have not. The company expects them to be approved by 2027.

Advertisement

Singapore Airlines’ Boeing 777-9s are expected by the second half of 2027, said Lee Lik Hsin, chief commercial officer. “We are working hand in hand and working very hard with our partners [the plane and seat makers] to make sure that we achieve those milestones.” Across the industry, planes are awaiting seats, or indeed awaiting certification. The bottlenecks in the production and certification processes exacerbate each other. The unveiling of the business class seats in the RECARO factory in Germany last year. The Age These delays have prompted airlines, constrained in their ability to get new aircraft, to resort to cabin refreshes to stay competitive. Qantas announced one for its 737s in 2025. This has set off a rush in demand for new premium seating, which has strained both the industry producing it, and the few regulators in the US and Europe who can approve it.

Advertisement

Singapore Airlines’ first-class cabins, for example, move away from the sameness, featuring an undulating shape, breaking rigid lines and creating an aisle that is curved, a rare sight on a jet. “The curve in the aisle unlocks more space for the passenger,” said designer Ben Rowan, of London-based PriestmanGoode, who is the mastermind behind the layout. “You’re not looking at office cubicles in a straight line. This is a much more curving, welcoming space.” Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, individual full-flat beds 80 inches in length and 30 inches in width, and adjacent seats that can transform into a two-seater sofa for daytime lounging are all features. The slightly hexagonal cabins allow passengers sleeping on the “lie-flat” beds to turn and place their feet on the floor, creating a sensation similar to a bedroom.

Advertisement

“When you sleep and you get up at home, what’s the first thing you do?” asked Lee, the chief commercial officer. “You turn to the side, and you sit on your bed. We couldn’t do that before. “Today we can, because the curved walls provide a little bit of space for you to put your foot down, and maybe collect yourself before you stand up.” A redesign of a cabin in a style that complements Singapore Airlines’ high service level aims to reinforce its position as a premium airline, one with the fortune of geography to pick up Europe-Asia traffic lost to its rival Gulf airlines when the Iran conflict began in February. The first class seat in full lie flat position, seen at the factory in North Carolina in the US. Chris Zappone Singapore Airlines flights from Australia to Europe gained 25 per cent more passengers in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the same time last year, with fares surging 109 per cent in that time, according to data from aviation data and analytics company Cirium.

Advertisement

Singapore Airlines’ refit itself was announced after it became clear the premium airline wasn’t going to get the 777-9 it ordered on time. Made by Collins Aerospace in the US, the first-class seats are the result of a nearly decade-long process. PriestmanGoode began designs in 2018. The long timeframe is partially because of COVID and partially because of cascading disruptions to manufacturing afterwards. Trying out a mock-up of the first-class seats last year in North Carolina. NIne New premium economy seats will have adjustable foot and leg rests, dedicated storage, and a cocktail tray for drinks.

Advertisement

Economy seats have a redesigned seat-reclining mechanism with better knee and shin clearance, as well as an adjustable headrest. RECARO’s final assembly line for airplane seats. RECARO For all the soothing subtle colours of first class, and the golds and browns Singapore Airlines has been known for, the airline has chosen a blue-grey colour for its new business seats. The business seat, designed by BMW Designworks and made by Germany-based Recaro, reclines into a 79-inch-long fully flat bed, replacing the diagonal set-up Singapore business class is known for. The meal tray, which is often one of the most troublesome necessities of a seat, drops from below the seat back, pulls out and extends.

Advertisement

Yet, the complexity of the seat – and its safety requirements – have further tied up and delayed supply chains which have come under intense strain since COVID, a time when demand initially shuddered to a halt, prompting staff exits, and the closure of parts makers. Editor's pick Updated

Aviation Qantas to raise airfares, cut flights as fuel costs rise by $1 billion Part of the bottleneck for cabins is the number of companies qualified to do the seat design and construction. As AeroDynamic Advisory managing director Richard Aboulafia said at a forum held in June: “There aren’t that many seat suppliers, and it’s a rather labour-intensive operation”. Aboulafia said a kind of groupthink had taken hold in the aviation industry as airlines decided to retrofit their entire fleet. Part of what makes commercial aviation so safe are the standards built into aircraft manufacturing; everything that goes into a plane must be tested and certified for use. That includes seats.

Advertisement

“So the supply challenges and the certification challenges are magnified immensely by these specific industry dynamics in the seating business,” Aboulafia said. With so many different seats designed and produced in the industry, testing requires time. To expedite matters, seat-maker Recaro’s factory in Schwabisch Hall, Germany, has its own crash-test facility. Seat-maker Recaro’s factory in Schwabisch Hall, Germany, conducts tests needed to certify seats. Nine A catapult hurtles a dummy in a seat across a track, while 10 cameras and sensors record the impact. In one violent action, the seat is tested and photographed. At this facility, a single business-class seat can run up to €100,000 ($162,000) for each test. Specific certifications can require up to 18 separate tests. Costs can run into the millions as new designs are proved safe.

Advertisement

There are other expenses: the materials that go into the seats must be controlled and checked, which means more testing for flammability. An unassuming factory in High Wycombe, near London, illustrates the scale of the specialist companies. The Sabeti Wain factory in High Wycombe, near London, where workers stitch together leather for aircraft seating. Nine Sabeti Wain, a family-run company, whose origin story begins when the founders fled the Iranian Revolution for the safe shores of Britain, is now a major producer of leather seat coverings for airlines. Employees at Sabeti Wain fill a factory floor, cutting, fitting and stitching high-end leather that covers first-class and business seating in planes. Employees hunch over sewing machines, doing detailed, skilled work. (The company also has factories in Dubai and the US).

Advertisement

Related Article Aviation How premium economy became the hottest real estate in the air Part of what makes this work different from standard leather work is the requirement to meticulously check and track every material going into the products. That level of manufacturing and safety detail underpins the attention to detail in the design, presentation and execution of the new cabins coming to the Singapore Airlines planes, the elements the carrier will rely on to keep inducing customers to pay premium prices to fly on it. title: This ADHD program was supposed to improve access. Instead, it’s heightened confusion
text:

Exclusive NationalVictoriaHealthcare This ADHD program was supposed to improve access. Instead, it’s heightened confusion Grant McArthur November 8, 2026 — 1:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. A state-run program aiming to reduce barriers to treatment and accelerate access to ADHD medications has run into immediate issues after a bungled Victorian government website directed patients to the wrong clinics. Premier Ben Carroll last Monday celebrated an easing of the rules that govern who can diagnose ADHD, with 150 newly trained general practitioners across the state now able to diagnose, treat and prescribe stimulants for the neurodevelopmental disorder. About 150 GPs can now diagnose ADHD under changes introduced by the state government, but a directory bungle made it difficult for some to be found. Matt Davidson Previously, only specialists such as paediatricians and psychiatrists could treat ADHD, leading to high costs and waiting lists of up to a year for the estimated 163,000 Victorian children and 320,000 adults living with the condition. But an official Department of Health website that went live on October 26 to direct families to clinics offering the new GP ADHD clinics included at least 15 services that are not accepting patients as part of the program – including one health service that is not even open.

Advertisement

Mental Health Victoria chief executive Phillipa Thomas. A handful of other clinics taking part in the program were missing from the directory, despite their doctors undertaking training from the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) as part of the government’s program. Mental Health Victoria CEO Phillipa Thomas said the confusion meant that non-participating health services were last week inundated with calls from people trying to make appointments for ADHD services that weren’t on offer. “Many callers were already frustrated at having been turned away from other incorrectly listed providers, and understandably people’s patience was pretty thin. You can imagine how the situation compounded over days; with increasingly distressed callers at one end, and increasingly distressed and overwhelmed health service staff at the other,” Thomas said. “It’s a disappointing start and a reminder that it’s not in anyone’s interest for significant policy changes like these to be rushed.”

Advertisement

The incorrectly listed clinics include some that do not offer GP services at all, as well as specialist services such as mental health and emergency units that do not book consultations. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Psychosis linked to ADHD medication on the rise, doctors warn When The Age contacted the department about the directory errors, a government spokesperson confirmed that “a small number of clinics” had requested changes to their listings on the ADHD care in general practice webpage. In the days that followed, 14 services – including clinics in Altona Meadows, Barwon Heads, Frankston, Moe, Port Fairy, and Wodonga – were removed from the list, while five others were added. One service – The Living Room, which provided support in Melbourne’s Hosier Lane for people experiencing homelessness – was only removed from the official list on Friday, despite having closed last month.

Advertisement

Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Victorian Branch Chair, associate professor Simon Stafrace, said it was vital to remove barriers for people to access ADHD care closer to home. “We urge the Victorian government to make sure the information is up-to-date as quickly as possible, so this important reform can be delivered as intended, particularly in communities where people already face significant barriers to accessing ADHD and mental health care,” he said. Loading The government denied that it had bungled the rollout, saying the directory changes included instances where ADHD-trained doctors had consented to the publication of their details before later requesting removals. “A small number of clinics requested changes to their public listings, which have been updated,” a government spokesperson told The Age.

Advertisement

Related Article Mental health Victorian GPs to diagnose ADHD and prescribe medication for it under new reforms The government has now asked the RACGP, which earlier this year oversaw the training of GPs involved in its program, to ensure doctors communicate with their clinics about their participation in the program and their public listing on its directory. RACGP Victoria Chair Dr Anita Muñoz said GP ADHD assessments were a positive step towards improving access, and that patients welcomed the move. “The Victorian Department of Health’s list of participating clinics is regularly updated to reflect local capacity. Clinics may request to be added as services expand, and removed when practices are no longer able to take on new patients,” she said. “The level of demand we’re seeing demonstrates why these reforms matter, and why we really need to train more GPs to improve access to care. Giving more GPs the skills and authority to assess and diagnose ADHD will help patients access care sooner, closer to home.”

Advertisement

Related Article Explainer

Mental health What’s ADHD and why are more adults being diagnosed with it? The Age last week revealed psychiatrists’ concerns that a growing number of patients are developing psychosis, including paranoia and hallucinations, after taking medication to treat ADHD. Rates of ADHD diagnosis have skyrocketed in recent years due to increased awareness of the disorder, leading to a surge in the number of Australians using stimulant medications. In response to rising demand and longer wait times, state governments have been easing restrictions on who can diagnose and treat the condition. In December, Queensland became the first state allowing GPs to diagnose and prescribe for ADHD. Since then, South Australia, NSW, Western Australia and Tasmania have followed suit. Victoria’s changes mean that since October 26, trained GPs can diagnose and treat ADHD in adults and children aged six years and over, in a move that Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said would save families thousands of dollars and up to a year of waiting time for an appointment.

Mark Nawaqanitawase has been with his new club in Japan for just one week, but Saitama Wild Knights attack coach Berrick Barnes says the former Roosters premiership winner is already impressing his new teammates. Nawaqanitawase is expected to make his debut in a pre-season game against Tochigi Honda Heat on December 5, leaving him with just over a month to adjust to a new language and culture. Mark Nawaqanitawase at pre-season training with his new Japanese club Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights Instagram But Barnes, the former Wallabies playmaker who also worked with Nawaqanitawase as an assistant coach with the national team in 2023, has no doubts the star recruit will be an instant success. According to Barnes, Nawaqanitawase’s exploits in rugby league, which also included a State of Origin series win with NSW, are mostly unknown to the Wild Knights’ Japanese squad members, given the small footprint the 13-man code has in the country.

Advertisement

But the winger’s arrival has still created significant excitement at club headquarters, even for a squad used to regularly training with World Cup-winning Springboks Lood de Jager and Damian de Allende. “The Japanese boys don’t even know who he is, that’s the truth” Barnes said. “I mean a couple might, just because of all of us foreigners. Loading “But I’ll say this, I’ve never seen foreign players get nervous [at the Wild Knights]. Like, you can get the best All Blacks in the world walking through the door and they’ll be just like, ‘Hey mate, how are you going?’ “But there are a few of them who are genuinely nervous and excited to have him [Nawaqanitawase] come in the building. So I don’t see that too often. I’ll say that.”

Advertisement

Nawaqanitawase arrived in Japan at the start of November, but has already impressed with his reintegration into rugby after a two-and-a-half year absence. “You can already see the leadership qualities [he has],” Barnes said. “He’s also got a positivity about him that breeds confidence in others; he genuinely believes not just in his own ability, but that of others and he gives others confidence. Mark Nawaqanitawase won his first NRL title with the Roosters. George Chan “It’s only taken me a couple of days to see that, and it’s such a rare quality. There are guys who are good individually but who don’t have that ability to inspire others... “He’s already watched some of our footage [before arriving], so Mark’s already so far ahead of where a lot of other foreigners start. It’s been really refreshing to see.”

Advertisement

After winning 51 Test caps, Barnes played for the Wild Knights from 2013 until 2018. Foreign players in Japanese rugby were rarer when Barnes arrived, and the former Wallaby had to learn enough of the language to survive on and off the field. Today, however, Nawaqanitawase will benefit from most plays being called in English, and having a translator at training. The multicultural squad includes English, Tongan, South African, New Zealand and South Korean imports alongside the Japanese players, some of whom also work for the club’s owners, Panasonic. Berrick Barnes worked under Eddie Jones as an assistant coach with the Wallabies in 2023. Getty The Wild Knights are based in the regional city of Kumagaya, which has a population of under 200,000. Barnes likens their location to the Brumbies in Canberra, and their winning culture to that of the NRL’s Melbourne Storm and Super Rugby’s Canterbury Crusaders. The bright lights of Tokyo are just 40 minutes away by bullet train, but the players live in a smaller city that allows them to build their own unique identity.

After a successful career as a player and coach at the Wild Knights, Barnes advice to any foreign player, including Nawaqanitawase, is simple: Embrace the culture, and let your actions speak louder than words. Related Article Updated

The Queensland premier has waved off questions about a $100,000 donation to the LNP from a developer who was recently given rights to development prime riverside land in Brisbane by the state. Lancini Property Group was among five developers picked to transform barren land at Hamilton on the river’s north shore that had been picked for the Olympic Athletes Village by the former Labor government. Premier Crisafulli said the donation followed the correct process. Matt Dennien Its chairman Laurence Lancini is on the government picked Games Independent Infrastructure and Co-ordination Authority Board, which recommended the other sites might be more suitable. His son, Lancini Property Group chief executive Tomas Lancini, was at the press conference in September with deputy premier Jarrod Bleijie to announce the land would be used for 13 luxury towers, centred by a business hub developed by Lancini, which will also have 1500 apartments.

Two months later, a family trust linked to the developers donated $100,000 to the Queensland LNP, the biggest donation of its kind since the government scrapped a ban on developers making political donations implemented by the former Labor government. Lancini Property Group is one of five companies to develop the Hamilton Northshore site. Queensland state government Defending the donation, which was revealed by Electoral Commission of Queensland disclosure logs, the younger Lancini said the family was “supporting the party that is supporting Queensland’s growth”. On Sunday, Premier David Crisafulli brushed off questions about the donation. “It’s a matter for the party,” he said.

When pressed about whether it was a good look for his government, the premier said the correct processes had been followed. “It’s been declared, as it should be, and that’s transparent,” he said. “That’s an independent process, and it’s declared as it should be, and that’s transparent.” The land pegged for the athletes village will be developed by five separate companies. Julius Dennis There is no suggestion of wrongdoing, illegality, or that the donation had any bearing on the government’s procurement decision.

Advertisement

Laurence Lancini previously told The Australian his Hamilton interests were on the authority’s conflict of interest register. The development on the land at Hamilton is being overseen by Economic Development Queensland as part of the government’s statewide push to supercharge construction on housing projects. “Economic Development Queensland is completely separate to GIICA and conducted an independent and rigorous process to select the five proponents who’ll transform Hamilton’s riverfront into a thriving precinct, instead of Labor’s unfunded plan to build an athletes’ village,” a Crisafulli government spokesperson said on Saturday. Labor’s ban was in response to a CCC recommendation that council candidates be prohibited from receiving developer donations due to the corruption risk. Football Australia will continue to assess security ahead of the Socceroos’ planned friendly against Jordan after an under-strength squad was named amid player concerns over safety. Tony Popovic’s squad was released at 10:30pm on Saturday night for upcoming friendlies against Qatar in Doha on November 13 (November 14, AEDT) and Jordan in Amman three days later. Loading The friendlies were initially meant to serve as preparation for the Asian Cup, which has since been pushed back from January to December 2027 due to security concerns in host country Saudi Arabia. Professional Footballers Australia on Friday said players had “overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated”.

Advertisement

Captain Maty Ryan and fellow veterans Jackson Irvine and Milos Degenek, plus midfielder Aiden O’Neill, are the most prominent omissions from coach Tony Popovic’s squad, which includes seven uncapped players. It is unclear whether those players made themselves unavailable for safety reasons. As yet, there has been no movement on the Amman fixture, despite Indonesia recently cancelling their own planned friendly in Jordan. Diesel Herrington, the younger brother of Socceroo Lucas Herrington, is in line to make his Australian debut. Getty Images “For the match against Jordan, we will continue to assess the security environment and provide players and staff with timely, comprehensive updates, including relevant safety advice and risk assessments,” FA chief executive Martin Kugeler said in a statement. “The safety and wellbeing of our players and staff remains our highest priority.” There are eight changes to the squad from September’s friendlies against Brazil in Australia.

Advertisement

New call-ups are Central Coast defender Diesel Herrington, older brother of Hull City ace Lucas Herrington, Portsmouth striker Thomas Waddingham and FC St. Pauli midfielder Sam Klein. Attacker Daniel Arzani returns after finding form at Ferencvaros, along with defender Gianni Stensness (Viking FK), who scored against Bayern Munich in the Champions League. View post on X Striker Kusini Yengi joins brother Tete, while goalkeepers Joe Gauci (Lincoln City) and Tom Glover (RB Omiya Ardija) have been recalled. “While the Asian Cup has been rescheduled, that does not take away from the importance of this window,” Popovic said in a statement. “We have limited opportunities to be together as a group, so every camp and every game is important.

Advertisement

“We will have an eye on continuing to evolve the squad for the future, with our World Cup 2030 qualifying campaign and the Asian Cup both now in the second half of 2027. This camp gives us another chance to work with new players and see how they fit into what we are building.” Qatar and Jordan were finalists from the last Asian Cup, and were viewed as ideal opponents for the Socceroos in their preparation for the next edition of the tournament. To remain in the job for the 2027 Asian Cup’s new dates – which take place over the Christmas and New Year’s period to avoid Ramadan, which begins on January 28, 2028 – Popovic and Football Australia will need to agree terms on a new contract, whether it be another 12-month term or encompassing the full World Cup cycle through to 2030.

Key points MUSIC: Courtney Barnett returns to the Palais for the first time since 2017

OPERA: This new production of La Bohème is a shiny successor to what came before

MUSIC

Courtney Barnett ★★★★

Palais Theatre, November 7 It takes three songs for Courtney Barnett’s Melbourne return to feel like 2017. The comical near-death experience of Avant Gardener was already an Aussie suburban classic when she played this esteemed venue nine years ago and again, every seat becomes a hastily abandoned inconvenience. Courtney Barnett performs at the Palais on November 7, 2026. Martin Philbey What’s changed? A slow churn of albums mapping the agonies of indecision, procrastination and rumination has culminated in the aptly titled Creature of Habit. “Feels like I’m going backwards, each day I preach my practice,” she rants in the opening blast of Stay In Your Lane. The backwards bit is an illusion. There’s more grey hair out here now and more confidence on stage. But Barnett’s three-piece grunge attack does feel as casually comfortable as her white jeans and T-shirt. It’s as if the stasis anxiety in her songs is exorcised in the act of simply doing what she does.

Advertisement

The bashful grin no longer tries to contain itself as she strolls to the lip of the stage to strangle those raggedly torn chords from her guitar. Our silence is “intimidating”; she squirms after the relative gentility of Mantis. But there’s very little of it as she interleaves ancient favourites with all 10 tracks from the new LP. Early EP tracks History Eraser and Canned Tomatoes (Whole) must feel like another lifetime to the singer, but from here, the consistency of her craft is striking. The same thread of restless, poetic self-examination is carried by a familiar racket conjured by unfussy bassist Bones Sloane and drummer Stella Mozgawa. It only takes three songs before everyone is on their feet. Martin Philbey Barnett gives herself and her overdriven guitar room to breathe in the slowed coda of City Looks Pretty and other improvised breakdowns, and the noise default is leavened by the likes of singalong favourite Depreston. The solo spell of Mostly Patient stills the beer-hoisting crowd like magic. The fact that any of the new songs might have fit neatly enough on her first album puts a lid on the evening’s surprises. But Barnett’s musical vocabulary is a reflection of an inner monologue that strives to accept what won’t change. “Reborn every morning, still somehow getting older,” she sings in a song called Another Beautiful Day. To her fans, the gift is in feeling the same. They’re still the kid in Elevator Operator and they know Nobody Really Cares If You Don’t Go To The Party like a thing only your best friend would tell you. Growing older hasn’t made any of us less ourselves. Some habits are just keepers.

Reviewed by Michael Dwyer

Advertisement

OPERA

La Bohème ★★★★

Opera Australia, The Regent Theatre, until November 18 Bohème is back, baby. And not the Gale Edwards production that returned in almost every Opera Australia season in the past 15 years, but a new, shiny successor. This new production of La Bohème is a shiny successor to what came before. Peter Foster Beloved by novices and veterans alike, Puccini’s La Bohème sits at the centre of basically every opera company worldwide. With Edwards’ loyal moneymaker put out to pasture, OA entrusted young Australian director Constantine Costi to make its golden goose anew. They could not have made a finer choice. Costi has assembled a brilliant creative team in fellow thirty-somethings, Dann Barber (sets) and Sabina Myers (costumes). There are many jaw-droppingly stunning moments: from Rodolfo and Mimi singing literally suspended in mid-air to the sheer scale of Café Momus. Visually, it’s everything you ever wanted in an opera.

Advertisement

The sound, regrettably, was less convincing. At no fault of young British conductor Finnegan Downie Dear, who led with passionate precision, nor Orchestra Victoria, who dutifully acquiesced whenever Downie Dear gestured for them to effectively turn it down. It’s the unforgiving acoustics of the Regent, where the orchestra is in front of the stage, rather than in the pit. But such is Bohème’s aforementioned perennial appeal, a revival – in another theatre – is not far away. Galina Cheplakova as Mimi and Kang Wang as Rodolfo. Peter Foster As bohemians Marcello, Colline and Schaunard, OA stalwarts Luke Gabbedy, David Parkin and Shane Lowrencev really do feel like old friends; their chemistry unforced. Making her hometown OA debut, Alexandra Flood (Musetta) is now, deservedly, on a Siobhan Stagg-esque trajectory, beloved at home and overseas. Flood has dynamo stage presence and shimmering vocals with perfect pianissimo high notes.

Advertisement

Tenor Kang Wang has long been an excellent Rodolfo, and Russian Galina Cheplakova’s heartbreaking Mimi was flawless, with the most beautiful array of vocal colours. This is what a national arts company should be doing, allowing inspired young Australian creatives to breathe new life into the classics. The art evolves and so too does our relationship with the piece. Costi’s Bohème will ensure that this tryst will endure.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
